meta.title: Harmonic Inc — Nimrod Ben-Natan's CableOS virtualisation pivot through the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle and the video software separation
meta.abstract: Harmonic Inc is a San Jose, California-based broadband and video technology vendor listed on the NASDAQ under the ticker HLIT. The company operates two principal business segments: Broadband, which provides the CableOS virtualised cable access platform (vCMTS) to cable operators including the substantial multi-year deployment programmes at Comcast and Charter Communications; and Video, which provides software-based video processing and delivery solutions for media customers. The 2019-2024 period was substantially defined by the CableOS deployment scaling at Comcast (the principal cable operator customer for the virtualised platform), the broader DOCSIS 4.0 transition cycle providing the multi-year forward Broadband segment demand context, and the strategic posture refinement separating the Broadband and Video segment operations including the announced 2024 spin-off planning for the Video business. Under CEO Nimrod Ben-Natan (since February 2024, succeeding interim CEO Walter Jankovic who had succeeded Patrick Harshman following his September 2023 retirement), the strategic mandate has been the CableOS deployment scaling continuation, the broader Broadband segment positioning through the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle, and the Video segment separation planning. The fiscal 2024 revenue was approximately $580 million reflecting the Broadband segment scaling combined with the Video segment trajectory; the fiscal 2025-2026 quarterly progression has continued the CableOS deployment scaling plus the broader Broadband segment positioning evolution.

chapters.title: Snapshot
chapters.body:
## A Company at an Inflection

Two decisions in quick succession redrew Harmonic's strategic map. In ~~February 2024~~ ==April 2024==, Nimrod Ben-Natan — who had spent ~~more than two decades inside the company since the 1999 DiviCom acquisition~~ ==nearly three decades at Harmonic since joining the company in 1996== and most recently served as senior vice president and general manager of the Cable Edge business — ~~took~~ ==was appointed to== the president and chief executive officer title at Harmonic Inc. (HLIT, NASDAQ) ==effective June 11, 2024==, succeeding ~~Walter Jankovic, who had held the post on an interim basis following Patrick Harshman's September 2023 retirement~~ ==Patrick Harshman, who retired the same day==. Harshman had led the company for ~~twenty-six years; Jankovic returned to his chief financial officer role under Ben-Natan~~ ==eighteen years, having been named president and CEO in May 2006==. ~~Simultaneously, Harmonic accelerated a formal review of its Video segment, eventually announcing its outright sale to MediaKind.~~ ==That same month, Harmonic concluded a formal review of its Video segment without a separation; in December 2025 it announced the outright sale of that business to MediaKind.== Together, the leadership change and the Video divestiture aimed to refocus a San Jose, California company — founded in 1988 — onto a single strategic proposition: that the cable industry's multi-year shift to Unified DOCSIS 4.0 would sustain and accelerate demand for Harmonic's virtualised cable access software.

## Two Segments, One Direction

Harmonic reported two segments. The **Broadband segment** comprised cOS™, a virtualised cable modem termination system (vCMTS) running on commercial off-the-shelf servers, together with complementary distributed-access-architecture hardware — including virtual Broadband Network Gateway, Jetty Remote Switch, and Ripple DAA node — and cloud orchestration tooling. The **Video segment** provided software-based video processing and delivery for broadcasters and media operators. As of the 23 May 2026 frozen snapshot, the Video segment was in the terminal stage of a $145 million all-cash sale to MediaKind (Leone Media Inc.), announced on 8 December 2025 and formalised via an Asset Purchase Agreement executed 20 March 2026 following French employee works council consultation. Closing was expected in the second quarter of 2026. [Source](https://www.harmonicinc.com/press-releases/harmonic-announces-pending-sale-of-its-video-business-to-mediakind)

Ben-Natan framed the rationale in one sentence: the transaction would "advance the growth strategies of both companies," leaving a post-separation Harmonic as a pure-play broadband access platform vendor.

## Revenue Arc and the DOCSIS Transition Trough

Harmonic's consolidated revenues rose from $377 million in 2020 to a record $679 million in FY2024, with the Broadband segment contributing $488 million and the Video segment $191 million. [(SEC EDGAR, CIK 0000851310)](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310)

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue ($M) | Broadband ($M) | Video ($M) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | ~~646~~ ==625== | — | — |
| 2023 | 610 | — | — |
| 2024 | 679 | 488 | 191 |
| 2025 | 571 | 361 | ~210 |
| 2026F | — | 475–495 | divesting |

FY2025 consolidated revenue fell to $570.8 million as the cable industry's pause ahead of Unified DOCSIS 4.0 commercial deployment compressed near-term Broadband volumes. Ben-Natan had pre-signalled the move at the FY2024 earnings call:

> "We're navigating a shift to Unified DOCSIS 4.0 in 2025, which will result in below-trend revenue due to timing, but we're maintaining our technology and market share leadership. We expect strong cash flow in 2025 and are positioned for above-market trend growth in 2026."

The recovery arrived on schedule. Q4 2025 Broadband bookings reached a record $346.9 million in a single quarter — a 3.5 book-to-bill ratio — lifting total backlog and deferred revenue to $573.8 million, up 73 percent year-over-year. [(Harmonic Q4 2025 press release)](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/HLIT/harmonic-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fiscal-2025-ksniufy4i1ch.html) In Q1 2026, Broadband revenue rose 43 percent year-over-year to $121.7 million; management raised full-year 2026 Broadband guidance to $475–$495 million. [(Harmonic Q1 2026 press release)](https://www.stocktitan.net/news/HLIT/harmonic-announces-first-quarter-2026-p6n817lbqhe3.html)

## The Comcast Anchor

Harmonic's CableOS deployment at Comcast began in 2018 and remained the franchise's commercial cornerstone. By the third quarter of 2025 Comcast accounted for 43 percent of Harmonic's consolidated revenue. The operator was adding roughly one million new fibre passings per year using Harmonic's converged cOS platform — spanning residential, commercial, and BEAD-funded rural programmes — with 1.2 million additional locations targeted by end-2025. [(Harmonic-Comcast announcement)](https://www.harmonicinc.com/press-releases/harmonic-and-comcast-work-together-to-expand-fiber-broadband-access) Across the broader industry, cOS was deployed at 127 operators serving 33.3 million cable modems at end-2024, with ten Tier 1 operators engaged on Unified DOCSIS 4.0 trials or early commercial programmes. At the Q3 2025 earnings call, Ben-Natan set out the competitive framing:

> "At this scale, the gap between Harmonic and the rest of the market has become extraordinary. Our field-proven consistency, operational depth, and nearly decade-long production maturity place our platform in a class of its own."

## Dossier Questions

Four structural questions drive the analysis that follows. Whether Comcast's roughly one-million-passings-per-year deployment rate proves durable as the operator manages its own capital envelope and competitive pressures. Whether Unified DOCSIS 4.0 adoption accelerates across the broader North American and international cable operator base in line with the record $582 million backlog Harmonic carried into Q1 2026. Whether the MediaKind transaction closes on schedule and delivers the full $145 million in cash — resolving eighteen months of strategic ambiguity around the Video segment. And how Harmonic defends its virtualised access platform against Cisco Systems, CommScope, Vecima Networks, and the Arista Networks adjacency entrants that have begun circling the cable access software layer.

---

chapters.title: From 1988 founding through DiviCom, Comcast CableOS, Harshman, Ben-Natan
chapters.body:
## Origins in Digital Video

~~Harmonic was incorporated in San Jose, California, in 1988~~ ==Harmonic was incorporated in California in June 1988, with headquarters in San Jose,== as a developer of fibre-optic transmission technology for cable television headend facilities. The founding thesis was precise: the analogue cable plant lacked the bandwidth and modulation efficiency to carry digital video services that operators and broadcasters were beginning to design, and the engineering gap required specialist hardware that the incumbent telecommunications vendors were not positioned to supply. The founding engineers built digital video encoding and compression systems at a moment when the commercial infrastructure for broadcast-quality digital distribution barely existed outside the laboratory.

The company listed on the Nasdaq under the ticker HLIT in 1995, raising capital that extended its sales reach into North American cable headends and European broadcast facilities. The mid-1990s were a period of rapid growth for the digital video encoding market: satellite operators were launching digital services aggressively, European regulators were mandating digital television switchovers, and North American cable operators were beginning the analogue-to-digital migration that would take the better part of a decade to complete. Harmonic was among the few specialist vendors with the engineering depth to supply multiplexers, encoders, and modulation equipment at the scale those rollouts required.

## The DiviCom Acquisition

The transaction that most durably shaped the subsequent three decades of Harmonic's trajectory was the acquisition of DiviCom ~~in 1999~~ ==from C-Cube Microsystems, completed in May 2000==. DiviCom was an Israeli developer of digital video encoding and conditional access systems~~; Nimrod Ben-Natan, who would become Harmonic's chief executive twenty-five years later, was among its co-founders and senior executives~~. The deal was valued at ~~approximately $780 million in Harmonic stock at announcement, one of the larger Israeli technology acquisitions of the first dot-com cycle~~ ==approximately $1.8 billion including merger-related costs==, and it substantially expanded Harmonic's engineering depth in MPEG compression standards and digital video systems integration.

Ben-Natan ~~joined Harmonic through the DiviCom transaction and remained with the combined company across successive senior roles over the following two and a half decades~~ ==had joined Harmonic in 1996, four years before the DiviCom transaction closed, and remained with the company across successive senior roles over nearly three decades==. His retention through multiple strategic pivots — from hardware-centric broadcast encoding through software-defined video processing and eventually to the virtualised cable access platform that became CableOS — gave him an unusually complete view of the company's technical heritage, product architecture, and customer relationships.

~~Patrick Harshman, who had assumed the chief executive role in 1997, oversaw the DiviCom integration and continued to lead the company through the subsequent cycles of the broadcast and cable equipment market.~~ ==Patrick Harshman would assume the chief executive role in May 2006 and lead the company through the subsequent cycles of the broadcast and cable equipment market.== His ~~twenty-six-year~~ ==eighteen-year== tenure made him one of the longer-serving chief executives among listed North American technology equipment companies.

## Building CableOS

The strategic inflection that would come to define Harmonic's positioning in the 2020s was initiated in the middle of the previous decade. Around 2016, Harshman's engineering organisation began development of what would become CableOS: a software-defined, cloud-native virtualisation of the cable modem termination system — the CMTS — that had historically been delivered as purpose-built proprietary hardware installed in cable operator headend facilities. The engineering thesis was technically radical for a market accustomed to multi-year hardware refresh cycles. A virtualised CMTS running on commodity off-the-shelf server infrastructure could, in principle, allow a cable operator to expand broadband capacity through software configuration rather than the laborious physical installation of proprietary chassis across thousands of headend sites.

The development period from 2016 to 2018 required close collaboration with a customer willing to commit engineering resources to a platform without commercial precedent. Comcast Corporation, the largest United States cable operator by subscriber count, became that anchor partner. The first Comcast CableOS deployment went live in 2018, representing the commercial validation of the virtualised CMTS model at an operator of genuine national scale. The deployment marked Harmonic's transition from a video equipment manufacturer with a cable customer base into something categorically different: a software platform company with the largest cable operator in the country as its principal scaling partner.

Revenue data filed with the [Securities and Exchange Commission (CIK 0000851310)](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310) shows the commercial impact of the subsequent deployment scaling:

| Fiscal Year | Total Revenue (USD millions) |
|---|---|
| 2019 | $384 |
| 2020 | $377 |
| 2021 | $499 |
| 2022 | ~~$646~~ ==$625== |
| 2023 | $610 |
| 2024 | ~~$580~~ ==$679== |
| ==2025== | ==$571== |

The acceleration from $377 million in 2020 to ~~$646~~ ==$625== million in 2022 tracked the broadening of Comcast's CableOS rollout as the operator moved beyond early-trial configurations toward full network deployment. By 2022 the Broadband segment, anchored by CableOS at Comcast, had become the company's dominant revenue contributor. Charter Communications and a broader base of domestic and international cable operators were added as customers, extending the platform's commercial reach beyond the anchor deployment.

## Gallagher, Governance, and the Harshman Retirement

Patrick Gallagher, a former senior executive at Sprint Corporation with deep telecommunications industry operating experience, joined the Harmonic board and assumed the chairmanship ~~in 2022. His arrival preceded by roughly a year the leadership transition that would reshape the company's executive structure.~~ ==in April 2013, more than a decade before the Ben-Natan succession reshaped the executive structure.==

Patrick Harshman announced his retirement as president and chief executive officer ~~in September 2023~~ ==effective June 11, 2024==, ending ~~a twenty-six-year~~ ==an eighteen-year== tenure that had carried Harmonic through ~~the analogue-to-digital encoding transition of the late 1990s, the DiviCom integration,~~ the video-over-IP pivot of the 2000s and 2010s, and the foundational years of the CableOS programme at Comcast. He did not depart the company entirely; Harshman remained on the board of directors following his retirement, preserving continuity of institutional memory at the governance level ~~through the succession period that followed~~ ==under the new chief executive==.

~~Walter Jankovic, who had served as chief financial officer, assumed the interim chief executive role immediately following Harshman's departure. The interim period extended across several months as the board conducted its succession process. Jankovic subsequently returned to the CFO function when the permanent appointment was completed.~~ ==Ben-Natan succeeded Harshman directly on June 11, 2024, with no interim chief executive in between.==

## Ben-Natan's Succession

~~In February 2024,~~ ==On April 8, 2024,== [Harmonic named Nimrod Ben-Natan](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) as president and chief executive officer ==effective June 11, 2024==. The appointment brought to the chief executive role a technologist who had joined ~~the company through the DiviCom acquisition a quarter-century earlier and had spent the intervening years~~ ==Harmonic in 1996 and spent nearly three decades== in senior product and operating positions, most recently as senior vice president and general manager of the Cable Edge business — the internal organisation that had built and commercialised CableOS through the Comcast deployment and the broader cable operator scaling.

Ben-Natan's succession was structured as a product-line-native appointment at the precise inflection point when the cable industry was entering the multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 technology upgrade cycle. DOCSIS 4.0 — the next-generation cable modem standard supporting multi-gigabit symmetrical throughput — required cable operators to upgrade their access infrastructure, and CableOS was positioned as the software-defined vehicle through which operators could execute that upgrade without reverting to proprietary hardware procurement cycles. Ben-Natan characterised the deployment opportunity in his early public statements as a long-duration structural demand driver rather than a short-cycle product refresh, emphasising the breadth of the operator upgrade programme still ahead.

Bart Spriester assumed the senior vice president and general manager role for the Cable Access product line organisation following Ben-Natan's elevation, providing operational continuity within the CableOS commercial programme. Jay Stein continued as chief technology officer across the Broadband and Video segments.

## ~~The Video Separation~~ ==The Video Divestiture==

Alongside the CEO succession, Harmonic ~~announced in 2024 its intention to separate the Video segment as a standalone business~~ ==concluded a strategic review of the Video segment in April 2024 and, in December 2025, announced the sale of the Video business to MediaKind==. The Video segment — encompassing the company's software-based video processing and delivery solutions for media customers, the direct lineage of the 1988 founding business and the DiviCom acquisition — had operated alongside the Broadband segment for the entirety of Harmonic's history as a listed company.

~~The separation announcement~~ ==The MediaKind transaction== reflected a strategic posture refinement that the revenue trajectory had made increasingly legible. The Broadband segment's growth through the Comcast CableOS deployment had progressively increased its share of consolidated revenue, while the Video segment faced the structural headwinds of a broadcast equipment market in secular transition as media companies shifted production and distribution workflows to cloud-native platforms. Robert Folliard, senior vice president of the Video division, led the ~~separation planning process~~ ==divestiture preparation== under Ben-Natan's direction.

The ~~post-separation~~ ==post-divestiture== entity — the Broadband-focused Harmonic — would be more narrowly concentrated on the CableOS platform, the DOCSIS 4.0 deployment cycle, and the cable operator customer base anchored by Comcast. The ~~Video separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture==, combined with the Ben-Natan succession, completed a repositioning that had been building since the 2018 Comcast deployment: from a dual-segment broadcast and cable equipment vendor into a focused virtualised cable access platform company at the centre of the cable industry's largest infrastructure transition in a generation.

chapters.title: Broadband (CableOS), Video segment being separated, and DOCSIS 4.0 context
chapters.body:
## The Architecture Shift: Software Replaces Silicon

For most of the cable industry's modern history, the cable modem termination system — the CMTS, the piece of electronics that sits at the headend and manages data traffic between the network and every modem connected to a given plant — was a proprietary appliance. Purpose-built hardware from a small number of suppliers handled routing, scheduling, and signal processing in dedicated silicon. Upgrading capacity meant buying and racking new boxes. Upgrading standards — from DOCSIS 2.0 to 3.0, from 3.0 to 3.1 — meant hardware replacement cycles that took years and cost hundreds of millions of dollars across a large operator.

Harmonic's CableOS product, launched commercially in the mid-2010s and put to its first major operator test with Comcast beginning in 2018, was a direct assault on that model. CableOS is a virtualised Cable Modem Termination System (vCMTS): it moves the MAC-layer functions of the traditional CMTS — scheduling, encryption, management — into software running on commodity x86 server hardware, the same class of machines that populate any hyperscale data centre. Physical-layer processing is handled by Remote PHY Devices (RPDs) distributed at the network node, completing a Distributed Access Architecture (DAA) that decouples where the signal is processed from where the intelligence lives.

The implications were consequential. A cable operator running CableOS could upgrade its access platform by pushing a software build rather than pulling and replacing rack units. Capacity could scale horizontally across additional COTS servers. Feature development — new DOCSIS modulation profiles, advanced scheduling algorithms, security patches — could cycle at software cadences rather than hardware procurement timelines. For an industry facing a generational standards transition to DOCSIS 4.0, the economics of that proposition would prove material.

## Comcast as Proving Ground, 2018–2024

Comcast, the largest cable operator in the United States, became CableOS's anchor customer and commercial proving ground. The deployment began in earnest in 2018, making Comcast one of the earliest large-scale operators to commit to a virtualised cable access architecture at production scale. By the time Patrick Harshman retired from the chief executive role in ~~September 2023~~ ==June 2024== — capping ~~a 26-year~~ ==an 18-year== tenure that had taken Harmonic from a video equipment manufacturer into the broadband infrastructure business — the Comcast relationship had become the defining commercial reference for the entire vCMTS category.

The scaling trajectory through this period reshaped Harmonic's financial profile. Revenue grew from $384 million in 2019 ~~to a peak of $646 million in 2022~~ ==to $625 million in 2022 and a record $679 million in FY2024==, a climb driven substantially by CableOS deployment volume at Comcast as the operator expanded the platform across its footprint. The Broadband segment, essentially coterminous with CableOS, became the company's growth engine, while the legacy Video business continued to generate stable cash flow from a global base of broadcasters and media customers.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD millions) |
|-------------|----------------------|
| 2019 | $384 |
| 2020 | ~~$377~~ ==$379== |
| 2021 | $499 |
| 2022 | ~~$646~~ ==$625== |
| 2023 | $610 |
| 2024 | ~~$580~~ ==$679== |
| ==2025== | ==$571== |

*Source: Harmonic Inc. investor relations; [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310)*

~~The post-peak moderation — $610 million in 2023 and $580 million in 2024 — reflected the natural rhythm of a large-scale deployment that had passed its most intensive rollout phase at the anchor customer.~~ ==Revenue eased to $610 million in 2023, re-accelerated to a record $679 million in FY2024, then contracted to $571 million in FY2025 as Comcast's most intensive CableOS rollout phase passed.== Charter Communications and a broader set of US and international cable operators represented the next tier of expansion opportunity, but had not yet replicated Comcast's volume.

## DOCSIS 4.0: The Upgrade Cycle That Defines the Decade

The cable industry's transition to DOCSIS 4.0 is not a single product launch — it is a multi-year, capital-intensive infrastructure programme that will determine which operators can credibly compete with fibre-to-the-home networks on symmetric multi-gigabit broadband. Two technical paths exist under the DOCSIS 4.0 umbrella: Extended Spectrum DOCSIS (ESD), which expands the upstream spectrum to 684 MHz or 1.2 GHz on existing coaxial plant, and Full Duplex DOCSIS (FDX), which enables simultaneous upstream and downstream transmission across the same spectral band. Both demand significant changes to plant infrastructure and, critically, to the access platform software.

This is where Harmonic's architecture thesis converges with a once-in-a-decade industry cycle. An operator running legacy proprietary CMTS hardware that wishes to support DOCSIS 4.0 must, in most cases, replace that hardware — a process involving substantial capital outlay and complex field operations. An operator running CableOS on COTS servers can, in principle, receive DOCSIS 4.0 capability through software updates applied to existing hardware, with incremental server additions to handle additional capacity. The distinction is not absolute — Remote PHY Device upgrades and plant electronics still require physical work — but the software-defined architecture compresses a significant portion of the upgrade cost and timeline.

Nimrod Ben-Natan, who assumed the chief executive role ~~in February 2024 following Walter Jankovic's interim tenure after Harshman's retirement~~ ==effective June 11, 2024 following Patrick Harshman's retirement, with the appointment announced on April 8, 2024==, came to the position having led the CableOS product line as Senior Vice President and General Manager. His operational familiarity with the platform — and with the Comcast relationship — provided strategic continuity at a moment when the DOCSIS 4.0 transition was moving from planning to procurement across the operator community. Ben-Natan had been part of Harmonic since ~~the 1999 acquisition of DiviCom~~ ==1996==, giving him a tenure at the company that pre-dated even some of the CableOS platform's foundational engineering decisions.

> "The DOCSIS 4.0 transition is a multi-year opportunity, and our software-based architecture positions us to be the platform of choice as operators plan their next-generation deployments."

The operator universe's pace of DOCSIS 4.0 commitment has remained a key variable for Harmonic's Broadband segment revenue trajectory. Charter Communications, which operates under the Spectrum brand and represents the second-largest US cable operator, has engaged with next-generation access planning, and its decisions alongside those of mid-tier operators will shape Harmonic's revenue cadence through the latter half of the decade.

## The Video Segment — A Parallel Business in Motion

Running alongside and largely independent of the CableOS business, Harmonic's Video segment has served a different customer set with a different technology stack. The segment provides software-based video processing and delivery infrastructure to broadcasters, streaming platforms, and media organisations — encoding, transcoding, content delivery network (CDN) functions, and cloud-native media processing workflows. It is a business with roots in Harmonic's founding-era identity as a video equipment company, and it has maintained meaningful revenue contribution through the transition to software and cloud delivery models.

The ~~2024 announcement that Harmonic would separate the Video segment as a standalone business~~ ==April 2024 conclusion of the Video strategic review, followed in December 2025 by the announcement that Harmonic would divest the Video business through a sale to MediaKind,== represented the clearest strategic statement of the Ben-Natan era: the company's future as a listed entity would be organised around the cable broadband opportunity, and the Video business, however valuable, was better positioned ~~as an independent unit~~ ==inside a dedicated media-technology operator== with its own capital structure, management focus, and strategic options.

The rationale was straightforward. The cable broadband and video processing markets have distinct customer bases, competitive dynamics, capital requirements, and growth profiles. A combined Harmonic was increasingly difficult to value cleanly, with analysts and investors attempting to apply different multiple frameworks simultaneously to a conglomerate with one foot in cable infrastructure and another in media technology. ~~Separation~~ ==The MediaKind sale== would allow the Broadband entity — essentially a DOCSIS 4.0-era CableOS pure-play with Comcast as anchor — to be evaluated on its own merits, and would ~~provide the Video business with the operational autonomy to pursue media-market consolidation, partnerships, or alternative capital structures without the constraints of a combined balance sheet~~ ==place the Video assets inside a media-technology consolidator with the scale and focus to pursue further integration in that market==.

## Strategic Refocus at the Transition

The arc from 2018 to the frozen snapshot of ~~May 2024~~ ==May 2026== traced a coherent transformation: Harmonic moved from a dual-business technology supplier into an entity whose identity was increasingly defined by a single large bet — that the cable industry's access infrastructure would virtualise, that COTS-based software platforms would displace proprietary CMTS hardware, and that the company which proved that model at Comcast's scale would be positioned to capture a material share of the industry's multi-year upgrade cycle.

~~The revenue contraction from the 2022 peak to the 2024 trough~~ ==The FY2025 contraction to $571 million from the record $679 million booked in FY2024== reflected deployment phasing rather than competitive loss, but it also underscored the concentration risk inherent in a business where a single anchor customer's rollout calendar can move consolidated results by tens of millions of dollars in either direction. Charter's trajectory, and the pace at which international cable operators engage with virtualised access platforms, will determine whether the ~~$580 million revenue base of 2024~~ ==$571 million FY2025 revenue base== represents a trough from which the Broadband segment re-accelerates into DOCSIS 4.0 spending, or a sustained plateau requiring a longer maturation period before the next volume phase arrives.

Ben-Natan's inheritance — a battle-tested vCMTS platform, a six-year Comcast deployment record, and a Video ~~separation~~ ==divestiture to MediaKind== in progress — placed Harmonic at an inflection point that its founders, who built a video equipment company in 1988, could scarcely have anticipated. The cable headend had become a software problem, and Harmonic had spent a decade arguing it had the answer.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, Comcast concentration, and the post-separation framework
chapters.body:
## A Six-Year Arc Shaped by One Customer

Few revenue curves in enterprise technology tell as concentrated a story as Harmonic's between 2019 and 2024. The company that Patrick Harshman had spent ~~two decades~~ ==nearly two decades== reshaping from a hardware-dependent video infrastructure vendor into a software-defined cable access platform reached its commercial inflection point not through broad market diffusion but through the progressive scaling of a single relationship: Comcast.

The aggregate revenue trajectory across the six-year period was one of ~~sharp acceleration followed by measured contraction~~ ==sharp acceleration through a brief mid-cycle pause to a 2024 record==:

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD M) | YoY Change |
|-------------|-----------------|------------|
| 2019 | $384 | — |
| 2020 | $377 | −1.8% |
| 2021 | $499 | +32.4% |
| 2022 | ~~$646~~ ==$625== | ~~+29.5%~~ ==+25.3%== |
| 2023 | $610 | ~~−5.6%~~ ==−2.4%== |
| 2024 | ~~$580~~ ==$679== | ~~−4.9%~~ ==+11.3%== |

*Source: [Harmonic Investor Relations / SEC EDGAR CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)*

The 2019 and 2020 figures — $384 million and $377 million respectively — represent the late-incumbent phase: a company that had already committed to virtualised cable access through CableOS but had not yet translated that commitment into top-line scale. The Comcast CableOS deployment, which dated to initial commercial trials in 2018, was still in limited rollout by then, generating engineering-services and early-licence revenue that moved the mix at the margin without yet dominating reported figures.

The inflection came in 2021, when revenue climbed thirty-two percent to $499 million. That move reflected a meaningful step-up in Comcast deployment cadence — the transition from trial to scaled production across a growing number of Comcast nodes. The gains in the Broadband segment, which houses the CableOS platform, absorbed the structural pressures in the Video segment, where secular headwinds from broadcaster consolidation and the migration of linear production budgets toward streaming were already compressing the customer base.

~~## The Peak and the Pullback~~ ==## The Pause and the Rebound==

The ~~2022 peak of $646 million marked the high-water mark of the initial Comcast deployment wave~~ ==2022 figure of $625 million marked the close of the initial Comcast deployment wave==. In practical terms, the Comcast relationship had by that point scaled sufficiently to represent a dominant share of Broadband segment revenue. Harmonic's annual filings with the [Securities and Exchange Commission](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310) disclosed Comcast as a customer accounting for more than ten percent of consolidated revenue — a threshold that, given the CableOS deployment profile, understated the operational dependency considerably. Within the Broadband segment specifically, Comcast was the principal contributor across software licences, SaaS fees, and associated professional services.

The ~~subsequent declines — to $610 million in 2023 and $580 million in 2024 — were not, in management's framing, evidence of platform deterioration. Rather, they reflected a natural rhythm in large-operator infrastructure programmes: an initial deployment wave generates elevated capital spending, followed by an absorption period during which the operator digests installed capacity before authorising the next tranche.~~ ==subsequent path — a modest dip to $610 million in 2023 followed by a rebound to a record $679 million in 2024 — was not, in management's framing, the product of platform deterioration at any point in the arc. The 2023 softness reflected a natural rhythm in large-operator infrastructure programmes — an absorption period during which the operator digests installed capacity before authorising the next tranche — while the 2024 record reflected the resumption of programme spending into the early innings of the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle.== Harshman, in the final quarters of his ~~twenty-six-year tenure before his September 2023 retirement~~ ==eighteen-year tenure before his June 2024 retirement==, repeatedly characterised Comcast's programme as multi-year in scope and explicitly tied the forward demand context to the DOCSIS 4.0 technology transition cycle then beginning to take shape across the US cable industry.

The concentration dynamic, however, was structurally notable. A company of Harmonic's size — ~~sub-$650 million in peak revenue~~ ==sub-$700 million in peak revenue==, San Jose-headquartered, listed on NASDAQ as HLIT — carrying a customer relationship of Comcast's scale created a bilateral dependency that shaped both commercial negotiations and investor perception. Positive Comcast programme updates produced meaningful stock movements; any signal of deployment deferral or volume softness had the inverse effect. The company's disclosures in successive 10-K filings acknowledged this concentration risk explicitly, as required under SEC rules, and the investor relations narrative over the 2021-2024 period was in considerable measure a running commentary on Comcast deployment phase and pace.

## Financing the Transition: Convertible Instruments

Funding the platform's build-out required capital markets access beyond what organic cash generation supported. ~~Harmonic approached its convertible debt structure in two tranches that bracketed the peak revenue years.~~ ==Harmonic's convertible debt activity in this window consisted of a single issuance, sized to bracket the early commercial-deployment years and ultimately retired in cash during the peak.==

In ~~March 2019~~ ==September 2019== — the same year the Comcast CableOS deployment was graduating from trial to commercial — Harmonic issued ~~$115 million of 2.0%~~ ==$115.5 million of 2.00%== Convertible Senior Notes due 2024. The instrument gave the company five years of fixed-rate financing at a cost below what traditional term debt would have required, in exchange for giving noteholders an equity conversion right at a premium to the then-prevailing share price. For a company at an early-commercialisation stage, it was a structurally appropriate mechanism: it preserved liquidity for platform investment while deferring equity dilution to a period when, ideally, CableOS revenue would have matured the equity value enough to make conversion economically logical for holders.

~~By 2021, with the revenue trajectory validating the CableOS thesis and equity markets in a receptive posture for growth-infrastructure names, Harmonic returned to the convertible market at scale. The company issued $230 million of 1.75% Convertible Senior Notes due 2026, using a portion of the proceeds to retire the shorter-dated 2024 notes while net-adding to its liquidity position. The 2021 transaction extended the debt maturity profile by two years and modestly reduced the coupon, capturing the rate environment of that moment. It also provided a balance-sheet cushion heading into what would prove to be the peak deployment years — ensuring that incremental Comcast programme demands on engineering resources, professional services headcount, and working capital could be met without returning to capital markets under potentially less favourable conditions.~~ ==Harmonic did not return to the convertible market in 2021 or in any subsequent year of the dossier window. The 2.00% 2024 notes remained the company's only outstanding convertible obligation through the peak deployment years, and the incremental Comcast programme demands on engineering resources, professional services headcount, and working capital were absorbed through operating cash flow and ordinary-course revolving liquidity rather than a follow-on issuance.==

~~The combined convertible stack — and the subsequent 2024 maturity on the original notes — gave the incoming Ben-Natan administration a defined liability horizon against which to plan the Video separation and post-separation capital structure. With the 2026 notes outstanding and the strategic refocusing underway, the treasury question of how to capitalise a standalone Broadband entity became one of the more consequential items on the new CEO's agenda from his February 2024 first day.~~ ==Harmonic settled the 2024 notes in full at maturity in April 2024, two months before Ben-Natan formally assumed the chief executive role on 11 June 2024. With the convertible obligation extinguished and the balance sheet effectively unlevered at the leadership transition, the treasury question facing the new CEO was less one of refinancing a defined liability and more one of how to capitalise the post-Video Harmonic without a legacy debt instrument to anchor the structure against.==

## The Separation Framework

~~The 2024 announcement to separate the Video segment was framed by management as a value-unlocking exercise rather than a divestiture of distress.~~ ==The April 2024 conclusion of Harmonic's strategic review of the Video segment — which culminated more than a year later in the December 2025 announcement of the sale of the business to MediaKind — was framed by management as a value-unlocking exercise rather than a divestiture of distress.== The Video business — software-based video processing, encoding, and delivery infrastructure sold to broadcasters, streaming platforms, and pay-TV operators — had been Harmonic's original franchise and remained a material revenue contributor through the dossier period. But within a consolidated Harmonic, the Video segment's secular growth profile, its customer base, and its capital requirements were structurally mismatched with those of CableOS.

The ~~separation~~ ==divestiture== rationale operated on two levels. First, ~~a standalone Video entity would be valued by public markets on its own terms — recurring software revenue, broadcaster consolidation dynamics, the shift toward cloud-based production — without the noise of a high-growth cable infrastructure platform distorting the multiple.~~ ==removing Video from Harmonic's reported results would allow public markets to value the remaining Broadband franchise on its own cable-infrastructure terms, without the noise of a slower-growing software-broadcast portfolio distorting the multiple.== Second, ~~a standalone Broadband entity~~ ==a Broadband-only Harmonic== would be free to pursue the capital structure, partnership strategy, and go-to-market posture that the DOCSIS 4.0 transition demanded, without the organisational complexity of running two businesses with fundamentally different customers, cycles, and competitive dynamics.

The financial framework of the ~~separation~~ ==Video divestiture==, as disclosed in the period ending at the dossier's frozen snapshot date of 23 May 2026, required Harmonic to report the two segments with sufficient stand-alone detail to support investor modelling of the ~~post-separation entities~~ ==post-divestiture Broadband franchise==. Within the Broadband segment, Comcast-related revenue — spanning SaaS subscription fees, software licences, and professional services — was the dominant line item, and the forward CableOS growth narrative was anchored to the multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle that cable operators across North America were beginning to fund. Charter Communications was cited alongside Comcast as a material broadband customer, providing at least a degree of diversification beyond the single-anchor dependency.

Within Video, the customer base was structurally more distributed — broadcasters, streaming platforms, and regional pay-TV operators across multiple continents — but the revenue was growing more slowly and faced secular pressure from the same forces compressing the global linear television complex. The ~~separation~~ ==divestiture==, in that sense, was also an acknowledgement that those two customer bases and those two growth profiles were better served by dedicated management focus than by the administrative co-existence that a diversified Harmonic had maintained for a decade.

## Ben-Natan's Inherited Ledger

When Nimrod Ben-Natan formally assumed the chief executive role ~~in February 2024, following Walter Jankovic's brief interim stewardship after Harshman's September 2023 retirement~~ ==on 11 June 2024 — succeeding Patrick Harshman directly, following Harmonic's 8 April 2024 announcement of the appointment==, the financial inheritance was a company generating ~~approximately $580 million~~ ==approximately $679 million== in annual revenue with a concentration risk in its highest-growth segment, ~~a convertible debt maturity approaching in 2026, and a separation process in active execution.~~ ==an unencumbered balance sheet following the April 2024 cash settlement of the 2024 convertible notes, and a Video-segment strategic review whose April 2024 conclusion was already pointing toward an eventual divestiture path.== Ben-Natan's prior role as SVP and General Manager of the Cable Edge business — the CableOS group — meant he arrived with direct knowledge of the Comcast programme's technical status and commercial cadence, a credential that was explicitly part of the board's rationale for the internal succession.

The revenue trajectory from 2019 to 2024 had demonstrated that CableOS could scale from pilot to production at a tier-one operator and generate transformative revenue growth. The ~~$262 million gross revenue gain between the 2019 trough and the 2022 peak~~ ==$295 million gross revenue gain between the 2019 trough and the 2024 record== was almost entirely a Broadband segment story, and the Broadband segment story was almost entirely a Comcast story. The task confronting Ben-Natan was to convert that proof-of-concept concentration into a diversified cable-industry franchise in time for the DOCSIS 4.0 capital spending cycle — while simultaneously executing ~~a segment separation~~ ==a Video divestiture== that would reshape the company's financial architecture from the ground up.

The ledger he inherited was not a failing one. But it was unambiguously a ledger shaped by a single commercial relationship, funded by ~~convertible instruments~~ ==a convertible instrument== timed to a specific deployment hypothesis, and now requiring a structural reset to realise the next phase of its platform ambitions.

chapters.title: Valuation — multiples, peer comparison, and bull/base/bear scenarios
chapters.body:
The gap between what Harmonic looks like in a rear-view accounting mirror and what it could become on the other side of the ~~Video separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture== defines the central tension in valuing the company at the frozen snapshot of May 2026. A stock that traded at peak revenue multiples during the Comcast CableOS scaling window has ~~endured three consecutive years of top-line deceleration — $646M in 2022 to $610M in 2023 to roughly $580M in 2024~~ ==absorbed a sharp FY2025 reset — $625M in 2022, rising into a record $678.7M in FY2024 before falling to $570.8M in FY2025== — and that revenue ~~drift~~ ==reset==, however ~~strategically motivated by the deliberate separation of the Video segment~~ ==much it traces to the December 2025 MediaKind sale that followed Harmonic's April 2024 conclusion of its Video strategic review==, has kept multiple re-rating elusive even as the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle builds.

## Current Multiple Snapshot

Precision on per-share market data as of May 23, 2026, is not available from public filings alone; what follows is reasoned from the last-reported diluted share count and recent trading ranges, and should be treated as indicative. [Harmonic investor relations](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) and [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310) supply the underlying financial inputs.

Harmonic's most recently reported diluted share count was approximately ~~78–82 million~~ ==109–110 million== shares. Against a trading range that, in the months leading to the frozen snapshot, oscillated between roughly $9 and $14 per share — reflecting DOCSIS 4.0 anticipation offset by Comcast concentration risk — a midpoint price of approximately $11.50 implies a market capitalisation of roughly ~~$900M–$950M~~ ==$1.25B–$1.27B==. Adding ~~reported net debt of approximately $120M–$150M (drawn senior secured facility and convertible notes, net of cash)~~ ==a debt-less-cash position near breakeven (the $115.5M 2.00% convertible notes due 2024 were fully settled in April 2024, and MediaKind divestiture proceeds remained pending at the snapshot)==, the enterprise value resolves to roughly ~~$1.05B–$1.1B~~ ==$1.25B–$1.27B==.

Against ~~2024 revenue of roughly $580M~~ ==FY2025 revenue of $570.8M==, that produces an **EV/Sales multiple of approximately ~~1.8x~~ ==2.2x==**. On an estimated adjusted EBITDA of $88–95M — a blended margin of 15–16%, consistent with recent reported ranges across the combined business — **EV/EBITDA runs to roughly ~~11–12x~~ ==13–14x==**. Forward multiples depend heavily on what the market assigns to growth: if consensus carries ~~2025 revenue recovering modestly to $600–615M~~ ==2026 revenue stabilising near $560–585M post-MediaKind== with margin expansion as the Video drag is removed, forward EV/Sales ~~compresses to approximately 1.7x~~ ==holds near 2.1x== and forward EV/EBITDA to ~~10–11x~~ ==11–12x==. Trailing P/E is difficult to compute cleanly given non-cash charges associated with the ~~separation~~ ==divestiture==; on adjusted earnings, with adjusted EPS likely in the $0.45–$0.60 range, the implied P/E sits between 19x and 26x.

The most analytically useful single metric for a software-infrastructure business in active transition may be the **pro-forma EV/Sales on the Broadband-only entity**. If the Video segment contributed approximately ~~$180–200M of 2024~~ ==$190.5M of FY2024== consolidated revenue, the remaining ~~broadband entity represents a roughly $380–400M base~~ ==Broadband entity represented a $488.2M FY2024 base, with FY2025 segment revenue likely a step lower==. Applying the same enterprise value — ~~Video separation may extract cash proceeds that reduce net debt~~ ==MediaKind divestiture proceeds, once received, would lower net debt further==, though the quantum remains uncertain at the frozen snapshot — the implied EV/Broadband-Sales ratio ~~rises to approximately 2.6–2.8x~~ ==settles near 2.5–2.6x on the FY2024 base==, a meaningfully different frame, and one closer to how software-infrastructure comparables trade.

## Historical Multiple Range

Harmonic's own multiple history reveals a pronounced compression cycle. During the 2020–2022 window, as the Comcast deployment demonstrated commercial viability and the Street began to ascribe SaaS-like re-rating potential to CableOS's subscription and usage-based billing model, EV/Sales reached 3.5–4.5x. Adjusted EV/EBITDA expanded into the high teens. That peak multiple reflected genuine optimism: revenue compounded from ~~$377M~~ ==$378.8M== in 2020 to ~~$646M~~ ==$625.0M== in 2022, a ~~71%~~ ==65%== two-year gain, while management guided to an eventual $350M–$400M ARR mix in the CableOS segment.

From mid-2022 onward, the narrative ~~broke. The revenue trajectory reversed.~~ ==turned choppier.== Comcast deployment volume, always lumpy given the capital intensity of node-by-node rollouts, normalised from the initial acceleration phase. ~~Revenue retracted to $610M in 2023 and $580M in 2024.~~ ==Consolidated revenue ground higher through 2023 and into a record $678.7M in FY2024, then collapsed to $570.8M in FY2025 as the Video review concluded and customer activity around the MediaKind sale weighed on the segment.== Multiple compression was ~~rapid: by early 2024, EV/Sales had retraced to the 1.5–2.0x range~~ ==delayed but sharp: through FY2025, EV/Sales retraced into the 1.5–2.0x range==, erasing much of the re-rating premium. By the frozen snapshot, the stock sat well below its 2021 highs despite the company carrying more strategic clarity — ~~Video separation announced~~ ==MediaKind sale announced==, Ben-Natan CEO succession settled — than it had during the 2022 peak.

The net result: Harmonic at the frozen snapshot trades at roughly **50–60% of its 2021–2022 EV/Sales peak multiple**, a de-rating that has not fully reversed even as the DOCSIS 4.0 transition cycle matures into a more tangible revenue catalyst.

## Peer-Group Multiple Comparison

| Company | Ticker | EV/Sales (TTM) | EV/EBITDA (TTM) | Fwd P/E | Rev. Growth (YoY) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harmonic | HLIT | ~~1.8x~~ ==~2.2x== | ~~11–12x~~ ==~13–14x== | ~20–22x | ~~–5% (2023→2024)~~ ==–16% (2024→2025)== |
| Calix | CALX | ~2.5–3.0x | ~18–22x | ~30–35x | Low-to-mid single digits |
| ADTRAN | ADTN | ~0.6–0.8x | NM (near-breakeven) | NM | Negative |
| Viavi Solutions | VIAV | ~1.8–2.2x | ~8–10x | ~14–17x | Low single digits |
| Ciena | CIEN | ~2.0–2.5x | ~12–15x | ~18–22x | Mid single digits |
| CommScope | COMM | ~0.5–0.7x | ~5–7x | NM | Negative |

*Multiples are approximate, derived from analyst consensus data proximate to the frozen snapshot, and should not be treated as precise.*

The table illustrates Harmonic's positioning: it trades at a modest premium to Viavi and CommScope — both carrying heavier legacy hardware exposure and weaker growth profiles — but at a meaningful discount to Calix, the most natural comparator as a software-defined broadband access platform. Calix's premium reflects its diversified operator base, lower customer concentration, and a recurring-revenue model that the Street values on an ARR basis rather than total revenue. Harmonic's discount to Calix is the single most important valuation gap to monitor: closing it, even partially, is the operating scenario that drives the bull case.

Ciena is an imperfect peer — optical transport rather than cable access — but instructive as a growth-inflecting infrastructure software business with a recurring service-revenue layer. Harmonic's multiple tracks Ciena's closely, suggesting the Street treats both as similarly mature infrastructure stories with moderate near-term growth potential, rather than granting Harmonic the software-inflection premium that management's ARR buildout narrative implies.

## Intrinsic-Value and DCF Framing

A simplified DCF clarifies what the current share price requires. Assume the Broadband entity exits the ~~Video separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture== carrying a ~~$390M~~ ==$488M== revenue base and achieves a 22–25% adjusted EBITDA margin as CableOS SaaS mix improves toward 40–45% of segment revenue. At a free cash flow conversion ratio of 60–70% of EBITDA, normalised FCF lands in the range of ~~$52–68M~~ ==$64–85M==. Discounted at a 9–10% WACC with a 3% terminal growth rate, the intrinsic enterprise value of the Broadband entity resolves to approximately ~~$870M–$1.15B~~ ==$1.05B–$1.40B==.

The current EV of roughly ~~$1.05–$1.1B~~ ==$1.25–$1.27B== sits ~~at the mid-to-upper bound~~ ==near the middle== of that range, implying the market is already asking for ~~near-perfect execution~~ ==solid execution== on the SaaS-mix transition with ~~minimal~~ ==limited== further Comcast deployment slippage. The current price is not a screaming discount to intrinsic value: it is a fair-value price conditional on the transition executing cleanly. The upside requires multiple re-rating toward the software-infrastructure peer group — 2.5–3.5x EV/Sales — which materialises only if ARR growth becomes the dominant financial narrative and the ~~Video separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture== is completed without stranding material enterprise value in the residual entity.

## Bull / Base / Bear Scenarios

**Bull case — $18–22 per share implied.** The DOCSIS 4.0 cycle accelerates Charter and Comcast node rollouts simultaneously through 2025–2027. ARR from CableOS reaches $300M+ by 2027. The Broadband entity, ~~post-separation~~ ==post-divestiture==, earns a Calix-like multiple of 3.5x EV/Sales on a ~~$420M+~~ ==$540M+== revenue base. Combined with ~~Video separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture== proceeds, the implied share price for the consolidated entity reaches $18–22. The critical enabling assumption: Charter deepens its CableOS commitment at a pace sufficient to partially offset Comcast concentration risk while international cable operators add further ARR.

**Base case — $11–14 per share.** Broadband revenue ~~recovers gradually to $410–420M~~ ==stabilises near $480–500M== by 2026, EBITDA margins improve to 18–20% post-~~separation~~ ==divestiture==, and the stock trades at 2.2–2.5x EV/Sales — consistent with mid-cycle infrastructure comparables. ~~Video separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture== completes without material asset-value leakage. The implied share price for the combined entity holds in the $11–14 range, representing modest appreciation from current levels and a steady re-rating as recurring revenue grows as a proportion of the mix.

**Bear case — $6–8 per share.** Comcast pauses or meaningfully slows DOCSIS 4.0 capital allocation, deferring CableOS revenue to outer years. The ~~Video separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture== faces execution friction — a dilutive transaction structure or extended timeline traps capital and compresses multiples. Broadband segment revenue ~~stagnates at $360–380M~~ ==contracts to $400–430M==. The multiple contracts to 1.5x EV/Sales as the Street loses patience with the ARR narrative. Implied share price falls to $6–8.

## What the Market Is Pricing In

The current multiple encodes a bet on orderly execution: Video out, CableOS ARR up, Comcast concentration stable or declining as additional cable operators onboard. It does not price in multiple re-rating to software-infrastructure peer premiums, nor does it discount a catastrophic Comcast slowdown. It is, in options terms, a low-delta position in both directions — fair value for a company in mid-transition, with asymmetry dependent on whether Ben-Natan's team can convert the DOCSIS 4.0 pipeline into durable, high-visibility recurring revenue before the market's patience exhausts.

The dossier's read diverges from implied consensus modestly in the bull direction. The structural under-penetration of virtualised cable access architecture across international cable operators — with the Comcast anchor deployment serving as the industry's reference architecture — suggests the current EV/Sales multiple undervalues the optionality embedded in a full DOCSIS 4.0 upcycle. The bear risk, namely a Comcast capex deferral, is real but, based on public guidance proximate to the frozen snapshot, does not appear imminent. The gap between the market's fair-value positioning and a fully re-rated software multiple is the execution distance Harmonic's management must close — and the DOCSIS 4.0 transition timeline gives them a credible runway in which to do it.

chapters.title: Post-Harshman quarters through Ben-Natan succession and Video announcement
chapters.body:
## The Final Harshman Quarters

Patrick Harshman had spent ~~more than a quarter-century~~ ==nearly two decades as chief executive== building Harmonic into the infrastructure layer beneath the world's cable networks. His departure in ~~September 2023, after twenty-six years~~ ==June 2024, after eighteen years== as president and chief executive, came not in crisis but in the quieter cadence of succession — a transition announced and managed, ~~the founder-era CEO~~ ==the long-tenured chief executive== stepping back as the company he had remade around virtualised cable access approached a new inflection point.

The financial record of his final years was not a clean crescendo. Revenue reached [$~~646~~ ==625== million in 2022](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com), an early plateau in the CableOS deployment ramp at Comcast and the broader operator base, ~~then retreated to approximately [$610 million in 2023](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) as the initial scaling phase at the principal cable customer moderated~~ ==then moderated to approximately [$610 million in 2023](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) before climbing to a record near [$679 million in 2024](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) as deployment activity at the principal cable customer reaccelerated==. The pattern was familiar to anyone who had followed the company since the 2018 Comcast deployment began: Harmonic's Broadband segment revenues moved in irregular pulses tied to capital-expenditure cycles at a concentrated customer base, not in the smooth quarterly progressions that analysts preferred. Harshman had spent years educating investors in that dynamic. His successor would inherit both the framework and its complications.

~~## Jankovic Holds the Bridge~~

~~Walter Jankovic stepped into the interim chief-executive role in September 2023 as the board initiated a formal succession process. The CFO's elevation was a deliberate stabilisation choice: Jankovic knew the financial architecture of the company intimately, held the confidence of the institutional shareholder base, and carried no ambiguity about the temporary nature of the role. His mandate was continuity — maintaining the Comcast relationship, keeping the Video segment on its operational path, and delivering clean quarterly disclosures while the board completed its search.~~

~~The search, as it turned out, did not require a lengthy external sweep. The candidate the board settled on had been inside Harmonic since 1999.~~

==## Lining Up a Successor==

==Harshman stayed in the chief-executive seat through the spring of 2024 while the board lined up an internal successor. There was no interim period and no external sweep; Walter Jankovic remained chief financial officer throughout, and the candidate the board settled on had been inside Harmonic since 1996.==

## Ben-Natan's Succession: ~~February~~ ==April== 2024

Nimrod Ben-Natan was ~~appointed president and chief executive officer in February 2024, and Jankovic returned to the chief financial officer seat he had vacated five months earlier. The symmetry of that return was itself a signal: the board had sought not disruption but depth~~ ==named president and chief executive officer by board announcement on April 8, 2024, with the role taking effect on June 11, 2024 upon Harshman's retirement. Jankovic continued in the chief financial officer seat through the handover. The board had sought not disruption but depth==.

Ben-Natan's path to the chief executive role ~~ran through DiviCom, the Israeli video-technology company he co-founded and whose 1999 acquisition by Harmonic brought him into the organisation. Over the subsequent two and a half decades~~ ==began at Harmonic in 1996, four years before the company's May 2000 acquisition of C-Cube's DiviCom division — a transaction valued at roughly $1.8 billion including merger-related costs — brought additional video-technology depth into the organisation. Over the subsequent nearly three decades== he moved through senior product and operating roles before becoming senior vice president and general manager of the Cable Edge business — the internal designation for the CableOS product line. He had, in effect, been running the franchise that defined Harmonic's forward strategy before he was asked to run the company.

The Cable Edge appointment made the succession logic transparent. CableOS was Harmonic's central commercial bet: a virtualised, software-native replacement for the proprietary CMTS hardware that cable operators had deployed for decades. The Comcast deployment, which began in 2018 and expanded steadily through the following years, was the proof-of-concept at the scale that mattered. Ben-Natan had been the operational steward of that programme before assuming the CEO role. The board was not installing a new strategy; it was installing the person most closely identified with executing the existing one.

Bart Spriester moved into the Cable Access general manager role that Ben-Natan vacated, providing continuity within the CableOS organisation. Jay Stein remained as chief technology officer, and Robert Folliard continued to lead the Video segment organisation.

## Revenue in the Transition Window

The quarterly record across the transition period reflected the structural dynamics of a company whose primary growth driver was tied to a single large customer's deployment calendar. Full-year revenue ~~fell from [$610 million in 2023](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) to approximately [$580 million in 2024](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) — a further contraction that, taken in isolation, appeared to tell a story of decline~~ ==rose from approximately [$610 million in 2023](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com) to a record near [$679 million in 2024](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com), with the underlying Broadband segment delivering $488.2 million and the Video segment contributing roughly $190.5 million of that total==.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD millions) |
|---|---|
| 2019 | $384 |
| 2020 | ~~$377~~ ==$379== |
| 2021 | $499 |
| 2022 | ~~$646~~ ==$625== |
| 2023 | $610 |
| 2024 | ~~$580~~ ==$679== |

*Source: [Harmonic Investor Relations](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com)*

The more precise reading was that ~~the $646 million peak of 2022 had represented accelerated Comcast deployment activity, and the subsequent two years reflected a normalisation in that cadence rather than erosion of the underlying relationship or the competitive position of CableOS~~ ==the $625 million 2022 print marked an early high in the CableOS deployment ramp, the 2023 step-down reflected a brief normalisation in capital-expenditure cadence at the principal cable customer, and the new 2024 record confirmed the underlying strength of the relationship and the competitive position of CableOS==. Harmonic management had consistently framed the Broadband segment in terms of multi-year deployment programmes rather than linear annual growth, and the ~~2023–2024 compression~~ ==2023 dip and 2024 recovery== was presented as consistent with that characterisation.

The structural point that mattered more, in Ben-Natan's first year at the helm, was what lay ahead: the industry-wide DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle. The technical standard's requirements — pushing cable networks toward multi-gigabit symmetrical speeds — represented the next major capital-expenditure wave across the North American cable operator base, and CableOS's software-native architecture was positioned as inherently better suited to the DOCSIS 4.0 migration than incumbent hardware platforms.

## The Video Separation ~~Announcement~~ ==Review==

The other defining event of 2024 was ~~the announcement that Harmonic intended to separate its Video segment from the Broadband business~~ ==the April conclusion of Harmonic's long-running strategic review of its Video segment; the eventual disposition — an outright sale of the Video business to MediaKind — was not announced until December 2025==. The Video segment — providing software-based video processing and delivery solutions for media and broadcast customers — had been part of Harmonic since its founding in 1988, predating the pivot toward cable access technology by decades. It was, in some sense, the original business: the compression and processing technology that had made Harmonic a name in the broadcast industry before Patrick Harshman had repositioned the company around virtualised cable infrastructure.

The ~~separation announcement~~ ==review's conclusion== reflected a strategic clarity that had been implicit in the CableOS investment thesis for years. A company with a large, legacy video business and a high-growth cable broadband platform carried a conglomerate discount; ~~separating the two would allow each entity to be valued on its own terms and managed toward its own investor base. Robert Folliard's Video organisation would pursue the separation process while continuing to serve the streaming and broadcast media customers that had been Harmonic's original constituency. The post-separation Broadband entity would be, in effect, the CableOS company — focused entirely on the cable operator market and the DOCSIS 4.0 transition opportunity~~ ==a clean break would allow each business to be valued on its own terms. The path the board ultimately chose — the MediaKind transaction announced in December 2025 — would leave the post-divestiture entity, in effect, the CableOS company, focused on the cable operator market and the DOCSIS 4.0 transition opportunity. In the interim, Robert Folliard's Video organisation continued to serve the streaming and broadcast media customers that had been Harmonic's original constituency==.

~~Ian Graham's~~ ==Timothy Chu's== legal organisation carried the corporate and contractual complexity of disentangling two segments that had shared infrastructure, sales relationships, and financial reporting for the better part of three decades. The Video segment's customer contracts, intellectual property, and operational systems required methodical separation planning across multiple quarters.

## Governance Through the Transition

Chairman Patrick Gallagher, ~~appointed in 2022~~ ==who has served as board chair since April 2013==, presided over the board through both the Harshman departure and the Ben-Natan installation — a continuity of board leadership that mattered during a period of executive change. Harshman himself remained on the board as a director following his ~~September 2023~~ ==June 2024== retirement, providing a channel for institutional memory that a clean break would have foreclosed.

The board composition reflected the company's dual identity in the transition period: ~~Mitzi Reaugh's media-industry background anchored the Video-segment perspective, while the telecommunications experience of Gallagher and the technology-operating depth of directors including Susan Swenson and David Krall framed the Broadband segment's cable-industry positioning~~ ==the 2026 nominee slate of Gallagher, Ben-Natan, Deborah Clifford, Stephanie Copeland, Dana Crandall, Neel Dev and David Krall combined telecommunications experience, finance depth and technology-operating expertise around the Broadband segment's cable-industry positioning==. The structure that Ben-Natan inherited was a company mid-transformation — ~~revenues compressing from their 2022 peak~~ ==revenues having moved from a $625 million 2022 base through a 2023 dip to a 2024 record near $679 million==, a ~~segment separation~~ ==Video-segment strategic review concluded in April 2024== in progress, and the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle not yet generating the next ramp. The first year of his tenure would be defined by holding the course while building the preconditions for what came next.

chapters.title: Ben-Natan, Jankovic, segment leadership, and Gallagher-chaired board
chapters.body:
## Succession by Design

The appointment of Nimrod Ben-Natan as President and Chief Executive Officer of Harmonic in ~~February~~ ==June== 2024 was less a hiring decision than the activation of a long-assembled capability. Ben-Natan had spent ~~the better part of a quarter century~~ ==nearly three decades== inside the company, ~~arriving through the 1999 acquisition of DiviCom — the Israeli multimedia encoding and transport startup he had helped build~~ ==having joined Harmonic in 1996== — and working his way through every level of product and operating leadership before landing in the role that mattered most heading into the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle: Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Cable Edge business, the internal organisation responsible for CableOS. When Patrick Gallagher, the non-executive Chairman, formally announced the succession, the board was not installing an outsider to arrest a crisis. It was handing the keys to the engineer who had designed the engine.

The transition unfolded ~~in stages across the autumn and winter of 2023-2024~~ ==as a publicly telegraphed handoff in the spring of 2024==. Patrick Harshman, who had led Harmonic for ~~twenty-six years — from 1997 through September 2023~~ ==eighteen years — from May 2006 through June 2024==, retired from the chief executive role in a planned succession. ~~Chief Financial Officer Walter Jankovic held the interim CEO position through the bridge period, maintaining financial discipline and operational continuity while the board completed its process. Ben-Natan's formal assumption of the presidency followed in February 2024, with Jankovic reverting to the CFO seat he had occupied before the interregnum.~~ ==The board announced Ben-Natan's appointment on April 8, 2024 with an effective date of June 11, 2024, the same day Harshman stepped down; Chief Financial Officer Walter Jankovic remained in the CFO seat throughout the transition.== The structure that resulted — a product-native CEO, a battle-tested CFO, and a chairman with deep telecommunications operating experience — reflected the demands of a company executing simultaneously on the largest commercial deployment in its history, at Comcast, while ~~engineering the formal separation of~~ ==moving to divest== its legacy Video segment.

## Ben-Natan: ~~Twenty-Five~~ ==Twenty-Eight== Years to the CEO Chair

Born in Israel and trained in computer science at Tel Aviv University, Ben-Natan ~~came to Harmonic at thirty-two years old as part of the DiviCom transaction~~ ==joined Harmonic in 1996==. [Harmonic Inc. Leadership](https://www.harmonicinc.com/company/leadership/) ~~DiviCom had been a meaningful force in digital video encoding and MPEG transport infrastructure during the late-1990s satellite and cable build-out; its acquisition broadened Harmonic's product line at precisely the moment that digital television infrastructure was scaling globally. Ben-Natan stayed.~~ ==Harmonic's roughly $1.8 billion acquisition of C-Cube's DiviCom division, completed in May 2000, broadened the company's digital video encoding and MPEG transport portfolio at precisely the moment that digital television infrastructure was scaling globally; Ben-Natan, already four years inside the company, would help integrate it.==

What followed was an operating career of unusual continuity for a technology executive in Silicon Valley. Through the company's Video-centric years — the broadcast and satellite era that defined Harmonic through the 2000s and into the 2010s — Ben-Natan accumulated product and programme experience across encoding, delivery, and network processing. His positioning shifted decisively when Harmonic made its bet on virtualised cable access. The CableOS initiative, which culminated in the landmark 2018 commercial deployment agreement with Comcast, required an organisational nerve centre capable of translating software architecture into cable-plant operations at scale. Ben-Natan was given that responsibility as SVP/GM of the Cable Edge business. In practice, this meant he ran the product line — engineering, product management, customer deployment, and roadmap — through the period when Comcast was integrating CableOS into its network and the broader cable industry was beginning to evaluate virtualised CMTS alternatives.

That background gave the ~~February~~ ==June== 2024 succession an asymmetric quality. Ben-Natan assumed the CEO role with a granular, operational understanding of the technology stack and the customer relationships that constituted the company's primary growth thesis. He was not arriving to assess an unfamiliar business: he had built the relevant portion of it. The mandate at succession was direct: sustain and extend the Comcast deployment, accelerate penetration among the broader cable operator customer base, and manage the structural evolution of the company — which included the ~~planned separation of the Video segment that Harmonic had announced in 2024~~ ==Video segment divestiture work that would ultimately produce the December 2025 MediaKind sale announcement==.

## Jankovic and the CFO Anchor

Walter Jankovic's career arc is the mirror image of Ben-Natan's in one important respect: where the CEO's strength is product-native depth in a single company, the CFO brings a cross-industry operating biography accumulated across several hardware-intensive technology cycles. [Harmonic Inc. Leadership](https://www.harmonicinc.com/company/leadership/) Before ~~returning to~~ ==taking== Harmonic's CFO seat, Jankovic held financial leadership positions at Lumentum, Oclaro, and Celestica — three companies whose fortunes tracked different phases of the optical networking and electronics manufacturing supply chains. He holds an M.A. in Accounting from the University of Waterloo and carries a CPA designation. The aggregate spans roughly thirty years.

~~The interim CEO period was brief — roughly four months between Harshman's September 2023 retirement and Ben-Natan's February 2024 appointment — but its significance was not trivial. Jankovic's willingness to serve in an acting capacity, and his orderly return to the CFO role when the permanent successor was named, established a tone of institutional stability during a period when the company was simultaneously navigating a CEO change, a major commercial deployment, and the early planning stages of a segment separation.~~ ==Harshman's planned retirement effective June 11, 2024 was paired with Ben-Natan's appointment announced two months earlier on April 8, 2024, and Jankovic remained in the CFO seat throughout — anchoring financial discipline as the company simultaneously navigated a major commercial deployment and the conclusion of its strategic review of the Video segment.== For analysts and investors, the message carried in the structure was clear: the management team was not improvising.

As CFO in the Ben-Natan era, Jankovic carries the financial architecture of a company in transition. The Video segment ~~separation — announced in 2024 and progressing through the frozen window toward a planned divestiture~~ ==divestiture — culminating in the MediaKind sale announced in December 2025== — imposes material demands on the finance function: carve-out accounting, standalone cost structure modelling, and the capital-markets interface for a transaction that, ~~if completed,~~ ==once closed,== would leave Harmonic as a pure-play broadband software company. Jankovic also manages the investor relationship alongside Ben-Natan, communicating a guidance framework to an equity market that, by the time of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, had extended the stock to approximately $15.20 per share against a fifty-two-week low of $7.80 — a doubling off the trough that reflected growing conviction in the broadband segment's commercial trajectory.

## Gallagher Chairs~~; Harshman Remains~~

Patrick J. Gallagher has occupied the board's chairmanship since ~~2022~~ ==April 2013==, arriving with a career biography rooted in the telecommunications operating world that Harmonic's CableOS business is now reshaping. A former senior executive at Sprint Corporation, Gallagher brought to the chairmanship an understanding of large-scale network infrastructure, carrier economics, and the organisational complexity of technology transitions inside incumbent operators — precisely the environment in which Harmonic's cable operator customers are operating. [Harmonic Governance](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com/governance) His tenure as non-executive Chair has encompassed both of the major governance events of the past three years: the Harshman retirement and the ~~Jankovic-to-~~Ben-Natan succession.

The Gallagher chairmanship's structural function during the succession was to provide stable governance continuity while the CEO seat was in transition. The Chairman's role in such periods is largely invisible when executed well; a CEO transition that produces no visible governance turbulence is itself evidence of a functioning board. That Harmonic moved through the Harshman-to-Ben-Natan transition without operational disruption — maintaining its Comcast deployment commitments and its financial communication cadence ~~through the bridge period~~ ==across the announce-to-effective interval== — reflects, in part, the board oversight that Gallagher provided.

~~Patrick Harshman's continuing presence on the board as a non-executive director, following his September 2023 retirement from the CEO role, is the most strategically significant single board composition decision of the transition period. A CEO who led an organisation for twenty-six years accumulates a depth of customer relationship history, institutional memory, and product knowledge that cannot be replicated from the outside.
