Harshman was present at Harmonic's transformation from a digital video encoding equipment supplier into a software-driven cable broadband infrastructure company; his board continuity gives Ben-Natan access, in the boardroom, to the full longitudinal context of that transformation. The arrangement is uncommon only in its degree: the former CEO as director is a governance structure that in theory creates awkwardness, but in a company executing on a multi-year technology deployment of the complexity and scale of CableOS, the institutional continuity benefit is material.~~ ==Harshman's June 2024 retirement was a complete departure from Harmonic; he does not sit on the 2026 board. Continuity at the top runs through Gallagher's long-tenured chairmanship rather than through retention of the outgoing CEO as a director, leaving Ben-Natan to draw on Harshman's institutional knowledge through informal channels rather than the boardroom itself.==

## Segment Operators and the Legal Function

Below the CEO and CFO level, Harmonic's operating structure as of the frozen window aligns executive accountability to its two reportable business segments. Bart Spriester, as Senior Vice President and General Manager of Cable Access, leads the CableOS product line organisation — the team responsible for the virtualised CMTS technology, the Comcast deployment programme, and the broader customer-facing operations of the Broadband segment. Spriester stepped into the role that Ben-Natan vacated on his elevation to CEO, inheriting a product line that had become the company's predominant revenue driver and its primary investment thesis for the capital markets.

Robert Folliard, as Senior Vice President for Video, leads the segment that Harmonic ~~announced its intention to separate~~ ==agreed to divest in December 2025 through the MediaKind sale==. The Video business — software-based video processing and delivery infrastructure for media customers — has its own customer relationships, technology roadmap, and cost structure, and Folliard's operational remit through the transition period has been simultaneously to maintain commercial performance and to prepare the segment for ~~standalone operation~~ ==handover==. That combination is demanding; managing a business unit toward a divestiture while preserving customer confidence and employee continuity requires a specific kind of operational steadiness.

Jay Stein, as Senior Vice President and Chief Technology Officer, provides the technology leadership function across both segments — a role whose scope narrows, in theory, once the Video segment is separated, but which during the transition carries the full product architecture responsibilities of the current dual-segment structure. Timothy Chu, as General Counsel, Senior Vice President of Human Resources, and Corporate Secretary, manages the legal and compliance framework; in the context of the Video ~~separation~~ ==divestiture==, Chu's function encompasses the transaction structuring, contractual carve-out work, and regulatory interface that a divestiture of this complexity demands.

## Board Architecture for a Bifurcating Company

The seven-member board that Gallagher chairs represents a composition calibrated, broadly, to the company's current strategic moment. Beyond Gallagher (telecommunications operating background) ==and== Ben-Natan (executive director)~~, and Harshman (multi-decade Harmonic institutional continuity)~~, the independent directors bring a range of industry perspectives. ~~Mitzi Reaugh contributes media and broadcast sector experience — directly relevant to the Video segment and its customer base of broadcasters and streaming operators, including through the separation process. Susan G. Swenson offers technology-industry CEO experience from prior public-company operating roles. David Krall adds technology-company executive depth. E. Floyd Kvamme, a long-tenured technology-sector venture capital veteran, brings the pattern recognition of someone who has watched multiple technology platform transitions from the capital formation side.~~ ==The 2026 nominee slate beyond Gallagher and Ben-Natan comprises Deborah Clifford, Stephanie Copeland, Dana Crandall, Neel Dev, and David Krall — a group whose collective profile spans finance, technology operating leadership, and capital-markets experience.==

The composition does not attempt to be a telecommunications-engineering board; it is a governance body calibrated to oversee a company navigating a specific set of strategic inflections — a major commercial deployment at scale, a ~~segment separation~~ ==segment divestiture==, a management succession, and a multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 cycle that is expected to drive continued demand for virtualised cable access infrastructure. ~~Against those parameters, the pairing of Gallagher's carrier-side network infrastructure experience, Harshman's Harmonic-specific institutional knowledge, and Reaugh's Video-customer-base perspective covers the principal board-level oversight dimensions of the 2024-2026 period.~~ ==Against those parameters, Gallagher's carrier-side network infrastructure experience anchors the board's view of Harmonic's cable operator customer base, while the broader independent slate provides the financial and operating perspective appropriate to a company closing out a major divestiture and executing on a multi-year broadband deployment.==

chapters.title: Comcast, Charter, broader cable operators, broadcasters, and supply chain
chapters.body:
The commercial relationship between Harmonic and Comcast Cable — the largest cable operator in the United States — defined the CableOS franchise as much as the technology itself. When Comcast agreed to deploy Harmonic's virtualised cable modem termination system at scale beginning in 2018, it did so under terms that bound the two companies far more tightly than a standard vendor agreement: Comcast received warrants to acquire Harmonic common stock, a structure that aligned the operator's financial interest with the success of the deployment and gave Wall Street a durable signal of commitment.

## The Comcast Commercial Architecture

The commercial agreement, disclosed in Harmonic's filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission ([CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310&type=10-K&dateb=&owner=include&count=40)), gave Comcast the right to purchase a meaningful stake in Harmonic at fixed strike prices tied to deployment milestones. The arrangement was unusual in enterprise software — closer to a strategic partnership underwriting than a procurement contract — and it reflected the degree to which the CableOS deployment represented existential stakes for Harmonic. A successful Comcast rollout would validate the virtualised access platform model; a stumble would imperil the entire broadband thesis.

By 2022, when Harmonic reported ~~$646 million~~ ==$625 million== in full-year revenue, the Comcast deployment had scaled to become the anchor contributor to the Broadband segment. The operator's cable plant — spanning millions of homes passed across markets including the Philadelphia region and parts of the Southeast — served as the living proof-of-concept for CableOS, demonstrating that a software-based vCMTS running on commercial off-the-shelf hardware could replace purpose-built cable access equipment at carrier scale. That demonstration carried commercial weight beyond Comcast itself: every cable engineering team watching the deployment was effectively watching a reference architecture take shape.

Comcast's concentration within Harmonic's revenue base also carried risk. Annual filings repeatedly identified the operator as a customer whose decisions — on deployment cadence, technology refresh cycles, or vendor selection — could materially affect revenue. When Harmonic's total revenue ~~contracted from $646 million in 2022 to $610 million in 2023 and then to approximately $580 million in 2024, the deceleration~~ ==moved from $625 million in 2022 to a record $679 million in 2024 before contracting to $571 million in 2025, the swing== reflected in part the lumpiness inherent in a deployment model where a single anchor customer's capital spending programme could swing quarterly results. The warrant structure, for all its alignment benefits, could not insulate Harmonic from the rhythms of Comcast's own network investment cycle.

## Charter Communications and the Broader US Cable Market

Charter Communications, the second-largest US cable operator by subscriber count, emerged as a significant CableOS customer as the DOCSIS 4.0 transition gathered momentum. Charter's network evolution strategy — oriented around multi-gigabit broadband ambitions and competitive response to fibre overbuilders — aligned with the virtualised access platform's promise of software-upgradeable capacity and reduced per-bit operating cost. Harmonic's filings listed Charter among its principal customers, and the operator's engagement provided the commercial validation that the CableOS franchise was not a single-operator phenomenon dependent on Comcast's continued patronage.

The broader US cable market presented Harmonic with a structural growth opportunity tied to the industry's technology replacement cycle. DOCSIS 4.0, the standard governing next-generation data-over-cable transmission, required meaningful capital investment by operators seeking to compete with fibre-to-the-home deployments by telephone companies. The virtualised approach that CableOS represented — decoupling the software intelligence from proprietary hardware — offered operators a path to DOCSIS 4.0 capability without the long lead-time hardware procurement cycles that had characterised prior generations of cable infrastructure.

Mid-tier US operators — those running regional cable systems with hundreds of thousands rather than millions of subscribers — represented a third tier of potential CableOS customers that Harmonic addressed through its direct sales organisation. These operators typically lacked the in-house engineering bench of a Comcast or Charter but faced identical competitive pressures from fibre incumbents and fixed wireless access providers. For them, the managed-software model of CableOS, in which Harmonic's engineering team carries the burden of platform maintenance and feature delivery, held particular appeal: they could adopt carrier-grade virtualised infrastructure without building the headcount to operate it.

## International Cable Operators

Harmonic's Broadband segment extended beyond North America to cable operators across Europe and Latin America. European cable markets — where operators including Liberty Global's regional subsidiaries ran large-scale hybrid fibre-coaxial networks — offered deployment opportunities as those operators contemplated their own transitions toward higher-capacity access standards. Latin American operators, in markets characterised by rapid broadband subscriber growth and more constrained capital budgets, represented a different demand profile: cost efficiency and deployment flexibility mattered more than outright peak throughput.

The international customer base provided Harmonic with geographic diversification that partially offset the concentration risk embedded in the Comcast relationship. International deployments also served a commercial purpose beyond direct revenue: they broadened the ecosystem of operators running CableOS, generating operational data and use cases that Harmonic's engineering teams incorporated into subsequent platform releases. In markets where regulatory or spectrum conditions differed from the United States, international deployments tested CableOS configurations that enriched the platform's feature set for the global operator community.

## Video Segment: Broadcasters and Media Customers

The Video segment — the business line that predated CableOS and that Harmonic's founders built through the company's early decades — served a distinct customer universe: broadcasters, streaming platforms, satellite operators, and sports rights holders requiring software-based video compression, processing, and delivery infrastructure. Names across the spectrum of global broadcast and pay-television appeared in the customer base, from national public broadcasters in Europe to North American sports networks to streaming services deploying cloud-native video pipelines.

The Video segment's customer relationships tended to be project-driven and technology-refresh-dependent: a broadcaster upgrading from standard-definition to high-definition infrastructure, or a streaming service transitioning its encoding pipeline to HEVC or AV1, represented a discrete revenue event rather than a recurring platform subscription. That structure produced a different revenue cadence than the Broadband segment's deployment contracts and contributed to the strategic logic behind Harmonic's ~~2024 announcement that it would separate the Video business as a standalone entity~~ ==December 2025 announcement that it would sell the Video business to MediaKind==.

The ~~separation~~ ==sale== announcement signalled that Harmonic's leadership — with Nimrod Ben-Natan installed as chief executive in ~~February~~ ==June== 2024 — viewed the two businesses as serving sufficiently different customer bases, capital requirements, and technology trajectories that operating them within a single public company imposed costs on both. For Video customers, ~~a standalone entity~~ ==a MediaKind-owned platform== would carry clearer strategic focus unencumbered by cable broadband capital allocation decisions; for Broadband customers, ~~the separated company~~ ==the post-sale Harmonic== would carry an equity story undiluted by Video's distinct growth profile.

## Semiconductor and Component Supply Chain

Harmonic's virtualised access platform model carried a supply chain profile meaningfully different from that of traditional cable equipment vendors. Because CableOS ran on commercial off-the-shelf server hardware rather than proprietary application-specific integrated circuits, Harmonic's semiconductor exposure ran through the broader merchant silicon ecosystem — Intel, AMD, and the network interface card suppliers whose components populated the servers that operators deployed in cable headends and hub sites.

The global semiconductor supply disruptions of 2021 and 2022 — which compressed inventory across the technology hardware sector — affected Harmonic's ability to fulfil hardware-related orders and contributed to the revenue dynamics of that period. Harmonic's filings disclosed supply chain risk as a factor in operational planning, and the company worked to extend supply commitments and diversify component sourcing to reduce single-supplier dependencies.

Over time, the shift toward a software-centric revenue model — in which software licences and SaaS-style platform fees represented a growing proportion of Broadband segment revenue — reduced, though did not eliminate, Harmonic's sensitivity to component availability. Software-only deployments, in which the operator supplied its own server infrastructure, sidestepped hardware supply constraints entirely. That architectural flexibility became a commercial argument in its own right: an operator facing hardware lead-time pressures could begin a CableOS deployment on existing or separately sourced hardware while Harmonic's software team managed integration and platform delivery.

The supply chain architecture also reinforced Harmonic's asset-light ambitions. Where traditional cable equipment vendors carried manufacturing facilities, component inventories, and logistics infrastructure, Harmonic's model pushed much of that burden to hardware vendor partners and, increasingly, to the operators themselves. The resulting capital efficiency — visible in the company's balance sheet relative to peers carrying heavier manufacturing footprints — reinforced the investment case that Ben-Natan and his predecessor Patrick Harshman had articulated across the decade-long CableOS build-out: a software company that happened to sell into cable, not a hardware company seeking a software veneer.

chapters.title: Where Harmonic sits against Cisco, CommScope, Vecima, Arista, and the broader cable access
chapters.body:
By the time Nimrod Ben-Natan settled into the chief executive's chair in ~~February 2024~~ ==June 2024==, the competitive map of cable access had already shifted in ways that his decade running the CableOS product line had helped engineer. The market Harmonic entered as a niche challenger in the mid-2010s had, by the frozen snapshot date of May 2026, reorganised itself around three vectors: a dominant vCMTS incumbent measured in tens of millions of managed cable modems, a distressed hardware-era giant scrambling to acquire its way into virtualisation, and a Canadian specialist collecting its first meaningful vCMTS revenue cheques. A fourth player — Cisco Systems — had effectively left the field.

## The Incumbent That Retreated: Cisco

For most of the DOCSIS 3.0 and 3.1 era, Cisco's cBR-8 Converged Broadband Router stood as the industry's reference CMTS platform. Cable operators from Comcast to mid-size regional MSOs standardised on it. The machine was well-engineered, well-supported, and, by the time DOCSIS 4.0 arrived on the horizon, a dead end. The cBR-8 carried no upgrade path to DOCSIS 4.0; the hardware architecture that made it reliable in one generation became a liability in the next.

Cisco did attempt a software-defined answer. Its cloud-native broadband router and SmartPHY virtual CMTS were developed under John Chapman, a DOCSIS pioneer whose departure from Cisco marked, in the view of industry observers, the symbolic close of the company's cable ambitions. By 2023, Cisco had quietly mothballed its vCMTS programme. The company that once held the largest share of cable headend equipment was, by 2024, no longer an active bidder for new CMTS contracts.

The vacuum this created was substantial. Harmonic's then-SVP Ben-Natan told industry publication Light Reading in 2023 that Harmonic was "poised to pass Cisco in CMTS market share" — a claim that had become plainly settled fact by the time he became CEO. Research firm Dell'Oro Group credited Harmonic with roughly 98 per cent of global vCMTS revenue as of year-end 2023. That is not market leadership in the ordinary sense; it is category ownership.

## CommScope: The Debt-Laden Incumbent Buys Its Way In

The more consequential competitive story was playing out at CommScope. The company had absorbed Arris International — and its storied E6000 Converged Edge Router legacy — in a 2019 transaction valued at approximately $7.4 billion. The deal saddled CommScope with a debt load that would define its strategic options for the next six years.

By 2024, CommScope was being categorised alongside Lumen Technologies and Dish Network as one of the most financially distressed equipment companies in the sector. Talks with an ad hoc creditor group collapsed in November 2024 without resolution. What followed was a $3.15 billion first-lien term loan and $1 billion first-lien notes refinancing, arranged through Apollo Global Management and Monarch Alternative Capital, to retire nearer-term maturities. The company did not file for bankruptcy, but the exercise demonstrated how little financial slack it carried into the DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle.

Its strategic answer to the virtualisation gap arrived in May 2024, when a bankruptcy court in Delaware auctioned the cable assets of Casa Systems. CommScope bid $45.1 million — outpacing Vecima Networks' $44.95 million stalking-horse offer — to acquire the Axyom vCMTS platform, along with Casa's fibre nodes and I-CMTS chassis. Axyom carried a modest but real production footprint: commercial deployments at Rogers Communications in Canada and Claro Colombia. Dell'Oro Group concluded that the acquisition positioned CommScope as the number-two vCMTS player globally, though it noted that both CommScope and Vecima had "lagged behind Harmonic" before the Casa deal closed.

CommScope also retained credible momentum in the physical-layer DOCSIS 4.0 market. Its vCCAP Evo cloud-native CCAP platform — capable of delivering up to 180 gigabits per second per rack unit on commodity Intel servers — won a significant European reference contract in June 2025, when Liberty Global selected vCCAP Evo alongside CommScope's DC2182 DOCSIS 4.0 1.8 GHz DAA nodes for upgrades at VodafoneZiggo, Telenet and Sunrise. That deployment covers the Netherlands, Belgium and Switzerland and represented one of the larger DOCSIS 4.0 contract announcements visible in the research window. Full-year 2024 revenue across CommScope landed at $4.21 billion, down 7.9 per cent year on year, though the Access Network Solutions division posted 11.8 per cent growth in the final quarter of 2024.

The balance-sheet story was not finished. In 2025, CommScope announced the $10.5 billion sale of its Connectivity and Cable Solutions passive-infrastructure segment to Amphenol — a transaction aimed at extinguishing the remaining debt overhand from the Arris acquisition. Critically, the cable access business was not sold. The Access Network Solutions division, home to the E6000, vCCAP Evo and the acquired Axyom platform, was retained as the core of the post-transaction company. The Amphenol deal, pending at the snapshot date, illustrated both the severity of the balance-sheet problem and CommScope's conviction that cable access remained worth owning.

## Vecima: The Specialist Building From the Node Up

Where CommScope arrived at vCMTS via acquisition, Vecima Networks built toward it from the access node outward. The Victoria, British Columbia company had established Entra as its Distributed Access Architecture product family — Remote PHY devices, optical nodes, and amplifiers — and over the prior two years had added an Entra vCMTS to the portfolio. Introduced in March 2024, the platform was cloud-native, containerised, and interoperable with third-party RPDs including Harmonic's own.

Vecima's first commercial vCMTS revenue arrived in the fourth quarter of its fiscal 2025, ending June 2025. A more significant signal came in April 2025, when Cox Communications — a Tier 1 North American MSO — announced a multi-year agreement to deploy Entra vCMTS for next-generation DOCSIS network modernisation, with commercial ramp expected to begin in Vecima's fiscal 2026. Cox's selection of Vecima represented the only confirmed Tier 1 US cable operator vCMTS award outside Harmonic's account book visible during the research window.

Full-year fiscal 2025 revenue came in at $285.9 million, essentially flat with the prior year. Entra DAA revenue of $222.7 million grew 5 per cent year on year but gross margin compressed to 38.3 per cent from 48.7 per cent, driven by product mix and foreign-exchange headwinds. The company cited the total vCMTS market at approximately $400 million over the following three years — a figure broadly consistent with Dell'Oro Group's projection of $367 million by 2028. On those figures, Vecima was entering a market it would largely share with Harmonic and, depending on CommScope's execution post-Casa, a third competitor.

| Vendor | vCMTS Status | Key Reference Customers | DOCSIS 4.0 Ready | Capital Position |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Harmonic (HLIT) | Commercial at scale; 146 deployments, 41M modems | Comcast, Charter, 140+ others | Yes — production validated | Strong; $573M backlog |
| CommScope (COMM) | Commercial via Axyom acquisition | Liberty Global, Rogers (legacy Casa) | Yes (vCCAP Evo + 1.8 GHz nodes) | Distressed; stabilising post-refi |
| Vecima (VCM) | Early commercial; first revenue Q4 FY2025 | Cox (contracted), 67 DAA MSOs | Yes (Entra vCMTS) | Revenue flat; margin under pressure |
| Cisco | Exited vCMTS | Legacy cBR-8 installed base | No | N/A for cable access |

## Arista and the Data Centre Adjacency

Arista Networks occupied a different quadrant of the conversation entirely. The San Jose networking company — $7 billion in full-year 2024 revenue, driven by hyperscale data-centre and AI-fabric switching — had no product overlap with cable access infrastructure. Its appearance in competitive analyses of Harmonic reflected a speculative thesis rather than a direct contest: as cable operators migrated headend functions to commercial cloud and edge computing infrastructure, the switching fabric inside those facilities increasingly ran on Arista hardware. CableOS, a software platform that runs on commodity servers, could in principle sit atop Arista-switched infrastructure — a vendor relationship, not a rivalry.

Whether Harmonic's software-defined cable access intellectual property could be adapted into AI data-centre or hyperscale routing applications remained, as of the snapshot date, a speculative investment thesis rather than a disclosed product roadmap. Ben-Natan did not address it explicitly in transcripts reviewed for this dossier.

## The Chinese Wall

The final competitive dimension was structural and regulatory rather than commercial. Huawei maintained a cable access product line built around DOCSIS 3.0 and 3.1 hardware, and its capacity for low-cost manufacturing had historically been cited as a long-term threat to Western equipment vendors. That threat was foreclosed in the United States when the Federal Communications Commission prohibited new equipment authorisations for Huawei products, with final rules effective in early 2023 under the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act. ZTE faced identical restrictions. No Chinese vendor appeared on any US cable operator's active vendor shortlist for the DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle. The regulatory barrier represented a permanent structural tailwind for Harmonic, CommScope and Vecima in the world's largest cable market.

## The Structural Gap

Against that backdrop, Ben-Natan's formulation on the Q4 fiscal 2025 earnings call was precise.

> "At this scale, the gap between Harmonic and the rest of the market is no longer incremental. It is structural."

The claim was arithmetically defensible. Harmonic managed more than 41 million cable modems and ONUs across 146 production deployments as of the same call. Its closest vCMTS competitor had booked its first commercial vCMTS revenue in the same quarter. Dell'Oro's historical data credited Harmonic with essentially all vCMTS revenue for the period when the market was being defined; the post-Casa CommScope and post-Cox Vecima were not so much catching up as starting the race. The DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle — with Dell'Oro projecting cumulative cable outside-plant spending of $10 billion through 2030, and 2026 expected to mark the capex rebound year after a 2025 inventory digestion pause — would test whether that structural gap was durable or merely a function of how long Harmonic had been alone on the field.

chapters.title: From 1995 IPO through CableOS, Harshman retirement, Ben-Natan succession, Video separation
chapters.body:
## The Founding Era and the Road to the 1995 IPO

Harmonic was incorporated in ~~1988 in Israel, where its~~ ==California in June 1988 and later reincorporated in Delaware in May 1995. Its== engineering roots in digital video compression and multiplexing reflected the broader technology wave sweeping the broadcast and cable infrastructure industry in the years after the analog-to-digital transition gathered momentum. The company went public on Nasdaq in 1995 under the ticker HLIT, [SEC EDGAR CIK 0000851310](https://www.sec.gov/cgi-bin/browse-edgar?action=getcompany&CIK=0000851310), positioning itself as a vendor to television broadcasters and cable headend operators at a moment when satellite, cable, and over-the-air broadcasters were accelerating capital investment in digital signal processing and distribution equipment.

The post-IPO business in the late 1990s was rooted in hardware and purpose-built compression appliances — encoders, modulators, multiplexers sold to broadcasters and cable headends. Revenue was modest and the competitive field was populated by Motorola, Tandberg Television, Scientific-Atlanta, and a cohort of European signal-processing vendors. Harmonic was a specialist, not a platform.

## The Harshman Era: ~~1997 to September 2023~~ ==2006 to June 2024==

Patrick Harshman ~~joined Harmonic as chief executive in 1997, eventually accumulating a 26-year tenure~~ ==was appointed President and CEO effective May 4, 2006, accumulating an 18-year tenure== that would make him one of the longer-serving active CEOs in the public semiconductor and video infrastructure sector. ~~His arrival predated one of the company's most consequential acquisitions: in 1999, Harmonic acquired DiviCom, an Israeli compression and digital video networking firm, bringing its co-founder and engineering leadership into the Harmonic fold.~~ ==He inherited the legacy of one of the company's most consequential acquisitions: in May 2000, Harmonic had completed its acquisition of C-Cube Microsystems' DiviCom division for approximately $1.8 billion including merger-related costs, adding compression and digital video networking technology to the Harmonic portfolio.== ~~Among those who arrived from DiviCom was Nimrod Ben-Natan, who would spend the next quarter century in successive operating roles before ultimately succeeding Harshman at the helm.~~ ==Nimrod Ben-Natan, who had joined Harmonic in 1996, would spend nearly three decades in successive operating roles before ultimately succeeding Harshman at the helm.==

Under Harshman, Harmonic navigated a structural inflection that periodically disrupts infrastructure vendors — the shift from purpose-built hardware to software-defined platforms. Through the 2000s and early 2010s, the company expanded its video processing portfolio for broadcasters, pay-TV operators, and media companies, building out an encoding, transcoding, and media delivery software stack that would become the Video segment of the modern Harmonic. Harshman repeatedly repositioned the product roadmap toward software, though the transition was gradual and the company remained substantially hardware-linked in revenue terms for much of the period.

## The CableOS Bet and the Comcast Anchor (2018)

The more consequential strategic inflection was the development and commercial deployment of CableOS, Harmonic's virtualised cable modem termination system (vCMTS). The architecture was a departure from the prevailing cable access model: rather than purpose-built CMTS hardware appliances from Arris, Casa Systems, or Cisco, CableOS ran cable access functions on commercial off-the-shelf servers, disaggregating software from specialised silicon.

Comcast became the anchor deployment partner and, by 2018, was actively scaling the CableOS platform across its network — a proof-of-concept deployment that would, over the following five years, become the broadband industry's principal commercial demonstration of a virtualised cable access platform at carrier scale. The Comcast deployment was not simply a reference engagement; it was the central commercial validation event that underpinned Harmonic's transformation from a video infrastructure equipment vendor to a broadband-access platform company.

The financial signature of the CableOS scaling is legible in the revenue trajectory. Harmonic's annual revenue climbed from ~~$377 million~~ ==$378.8 million== in 2020 to $499 million in 2021 and then to ~~a peak of $646 million~~ ==approximately $625.0 million== in 2022, with CableOS deployments at Comcast the principal driver of the Broadband segment's expansion.

| Fiscal Year | Revenue (USD millions) |
|---|---|
| 2019 | $384 |
| 2020 | ~~$377~~ ==$379== |
| 2021 | $499 |
| 2022 | ~~$646~~ ==$625== |
| 2023 | $610 |
| 2024 | ~~$580~~ ==$679== |

*Source: [Harmonic Investor Relations](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com), SEC EDGAR*

## The Harshman Retirement ~~and the Jankovic Bridge (September 2023)~~ ==and Direct Succession (June 2024)==

Harshman retired from the CEO role ~~in September 2023 after 26 years~~ ==effective June 11, 2024 after 18 years==, transitioning to the board as a continuing director — a structural choice that kept his operational knowledge accessible to the organisation at the governance level without interposing it into day-to-day execution. ~~The board named Walter Jankovic, Harmonic's CFO, as interim chief executive for the transitional period.~~ ==The board executed a direct handoff to Nimrod Ben-Natan on the same effective date, without an interim CEO period.==

~~The interim arrangement lasted approximately five months. Jankovic, whose CFO background gave him operational continuity without deep product-line ownership of the CableOS business, managed the bridge period as the board ran the succession process. His appointment was a stabilisation measure rather than an independent strategic mandate, and he returned to the CFO role once the successor was confirmed.~~

## Ben-Natan Succession: ~~February 2024~~ ==April 2024 Announcement, June 2024 Effective==

The board ~~named~~ ==announced the appointment of== Nimrod Ben-Natan ==as== President and Chief Executive Officer ~~in February 2024~~ ==on April 8, 2024, with the appointment taking effect on June 11, 2024==, [Harmonic IR](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com/governance). The choice reflected a deliberate logic: Ben-Natan had spent his entire Harmonic career — ~~from the 1999 DiviCom acquisition forward~~ ==since joining the company in 1996== — inside the company's operating structure, and had most recently served as Senior Vice President and General Manager of the Cable Edge business, the organisational home of the CableOS product line.

That product-line proximity was the thesis of the succession. Harmonic was entering the multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade cycle, a cable industry technology transition that would require every major North American cable operator to re-architect their broadband access infrastructure. Ben-Natan's mandate was to scale CableOS deployments not only at Comcast but across a broader operator customer base — Charter Communications among them — as the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle widened the addressable opportunity.

Speaking to analysts following his appointment, Ben-Natan framed the company's position as one in which the foundational commercial proof was in place and the task ahead was operational scaling rather than platform invention. The CableOS architecture had been validated in production at the world's largest cable operator; what remained was broader network penetration in a favourable technology upgrade window.

## Video ~~Separation~~ ==Divestiture==: Strategic Posture Refinement ~~(2024)~~ ==(2024-2025)==

In parallel with the CEO succession, Harmonic ~~in 2024 announced its intention to separate the Video segment as a standalone business~~ ==concluded a strategic review of the Video segment in April 2024 and ultimately announced the sale of the Video business to MediaKind in December 2025==. The Video segment — encompassing software-based video processing, encoding, transcoding, and media delivery solutions for broadcasters and media companies — had for years operated as a structurally distinct business alongside the Broadband segment, sharing corporate infrastructure but serving a different customer base and operating under different competitive dynamics.

The announced ~~separation~~ ==divestiture== reflected the evolved strategic posture that had been building since the CableOS commercial scaling: Harmonic's equity story, its analyst following, and its principal capital allocation priority had progressively re-centred on the cable broadband platform, and the Video segment carried valuation and resource-allocation friction inside a combined structure. Robert Folliard, Senior Vice President of Video, was assigned operational responsibility for the ~~separation~~ ==divestiture== planning within Harmonic's executive structure.

The ~~2024 revenue of approximately $580 million — down from the $646 million 2022 peak, reflecting post-peak deployment cadence at Comcast~~ ==2024 revenue of approximately $678.7 million — a record annual result, with the consolidated step-down to $570.8 million coming in FY2025== framed the financial context in which Ben-Natan entered the CEO role and the Video ~~separation~~ ==divestiture== planning commenced. The Broadband-first entity that would emerge from the ~~separation~~ ==divestiture== would be a more focused expression of the bet Harshman and Ben-Natan had made across three decades: that virtualised, software-defined cable access was a durable structural disruption, not a niche experiment.

chapters.title: CableOS virtualisation, DOCSIS 4.0 support, broader patents
chapters.body:
## The Virtual Stack: Software-Defined Cable Access

When Harmonic introduced CableOS in the autumn of 2016, the architecture it proposed was a fundamental departure from three decades of cable engineering convention. A cable modem termination system — the CMTS — had always been a proprietary chassis: racks of vendor-specific line cards, ASICs, and control planes locked together by the manufacturer. CableOS dissolved that hardware boundary, replacing the entire CMTS stack with software running on commercial off-the-shelf x86 servers and moving the physics of the network to standardised Remote PHY Devices at the node edge. The platform was cloud-native from an early stage, deploying containerised microservices orchestrated by Kubernetes and drawing on 4th-generation Intel Xeon Scalable processors for the signal-processing workloads that had previously demanded custom silicon.

The practical claims Harmonic made for this architecture were stark. Relative to a traditional CMTS, the company documented a 20-to-1 reduction in rack footprint and, across seven successive generations of commodity server hardware, a 75 per cent reduction in power consumption. Because the software abstracted the data plane from any specific processor, every Intel die-shrink translated automatically into additional DOCSIS capacity per rack unit — a compounding efficiency that proprietary hardware could not match.

## A Patent Foundation for the Virtualisation Era

The intellectual-property strategy that accompanied CableOS reflected the company's conviction that the virtualisation approach was architecturally novel. On 26 July 2018, the United States Patent and Trademark Office granted US Patent 10,020,962, titled "Virtual Converged Cable Access Platform (CCAP) Core." It was the first of what then-chief executive Patrick Harshman described as a broadening moat.

> "The future of cable access technology is virtualized software, and the award of this foundational patent highlights Harmonic's ground-breaking innovation and increasingly strong market position. This patent and our 94 pending patent applications, a number of which relate to our CableOS technologies, make a clear statement of our ability to solve the real-world challenges for our customers."
>
> — Patrick Harshman, press release, 26 July 2018

A second foundational patent followed on 4 December 2018: US Patent 10,104,405, covering dynamic allocation of CPU cycles in cloud-based video stream processing — a method central to Harmonic's Video-as-a-Service platform. By the time the [FY2025 10-K](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/0000851310/000119312526067506/hlit-20251231.htm) was filed in early 2026, Harmonic's active portfolio comprised 65 issued US patents, seven issued foreign patents, and 39 pending applications across cable access virtualisation, distributed access architecture, remote PHY, and video encoding.

Two later patents illustrated how the portfolio continued to evolve alongside deployments at scale. The company's patented PTP-less timing solution — which eliminated the need for Precision Time Protocol infrastructure in distributed access networks, reducing deployment complexity and lowering operator cost — became a documented differentiator in competitive sales. Polish operator Vectra cited it explicitly when selecting Harmonic for its broadband transformation in 2025. By then, chief executive Nimrod Ben-Natan described the solution going into commercial production as delivering a concrete economic benefit:

> "our patented PTP less timing solution into live commercial service. This technology lowers overall DAA cost."
>
> — Nimrod Ben-Natan, Q1 2025 earnings call, 28 April 2025

At SCTE TechExpo 2025, Harmonic also unveiled Pathfinder, a self-healing network capability that Ben-Natan described as patent-pending, designed to detect and mitigate localised spectrum interference autonomously — a foretaste of the autonomous network intelligence layer the company began presenting as a distinct competitive dimension.

The portfolio's only significant defensive test had come from outside the cable segment entirely: Avid Technology brought two suits in Delaware between 2011 and 2017 over data-storage patents relating to Harmonic's legacy MediaGrid broadcast storage product. After the Federal Circuit ordered a retrial in 2016, the parties settled in October 2017 on terms that included a cross-licence and a cash payment from Harmonic to Avid. The dispute touched no CableOS-related technology.

## Extending the Spectrum: DOCSIS 4.0 in Two Flavours

DOCSIS 4.0 arrived in two technically distinct variants that placed different demands on operators' existing hybrid-fibre-coax plants. Extended Spectrum DOCSIS pushed the downstream spectrum ceiling to 1.2 GHz or 1.8 GHz using conventional frequency-division duplexing — a comparatively straightforward amplifier upgrade. Full Duplex DOCSIS allowed simultaneous upstream and downstream transmission within an overlapping spectrum band, offering substantially higher upstream capacity but requiring amplifiers capable of managing echo cancellation at each node. Most vendors chose to support one variant or the other.

In October 2023, Harmonic announced that its renamed cOS platform had become the first in the industry to support both FDX and ESD within a single software instance, alongside 10G passive optical network convergence. The capability was demonstrated in live production with Comcast, whose chief network officer Elad Nafshi noted that the virtual CMTS deployment had positioned the operator to launch "the world's first DOCSIS 4.0-powered Internet service." Harmonic's own framing emphasised the strategic latitude the unified approach gave operators:

> "The cOS platform is unique in the marketplace today, making it even easier for operators to address the very real economic, environmental and technical requirements they face, while also ensuring greater agility and versatility to strategically extend high-speed services to more subscribers."
>
> — Nimrod Ben-Natan, press release, 16 October 2023

Hardware support for the new standard was delivered through the Pebble-2 Remote PHY Device, which Harmonic characterised as the most power-efficient device in its class and which supported DOCSIS 3.1 and both DOCSIS 4.0 modes across a full 1.8 GHz spectrum. On 8 July 2025, a Pebble-2 paired with the cOS core software achieved 14 Gbps downstream throughput at a [CableLabs interoperability event](https://www.harmonicinc.com/press-releases/harmonic-14gbps-docsis4-harmonic-cablelabs-demo) — exceeding the 10 Gbps headline target associated with the standard.

Field commitments followed the technical validation. By the close of 2024, Harmonic counted ten Tier-1 operators engaged on the Unified DOCSIS 4.0 platform. The first commercial Extended Spectrum rollouts entered service in the third quarter of 2025. Vodafone Germany completed a field validation before the end of that year.

## R&D Investment and Engineering Geography

The research expenditure that underpinned both the CableOS platform and the video portfolio was sustained at elevated levels through the growth phase of the DOCSIS transition. Combined R&D reached $126.3 million in fiscal 2023 and $121.0 million in fiscal 2024, representing approximately 18–21 per cent of total revenue in each year. The company's engineering footprint spread across sites in California, Oregon, and New Jersey in the United States, alongside significant presences in France, Israel, and Hong Kong, with supplemental development resources in Ukraine and India. France, in particular, generated meaningful cost offsets: the Crédit d'Impôt Recherche programme returned between $5.4 million and $6.2 million annually in tax credits across the 2021–2023 period.

After Harmonic announced the pending sale of its Video business to MediaKind for approximately $145 million in December 2025, the Video segment was reclassified as discontinued operations, and the reported R&D figure for fiscal 2025 — against continuing broadband operations only — fell to $75.0 million, with the roughly $45–50 million attributable to video processing engineering departing with the asset. The PURE Compression Engine, which had encoded content to HEVC, AV1, and VVC standards, and the VOS 360 cloud video platform carrying its associated processing patents, transferred to MediaKind upon closing. What remained was a tighter, broadband-focused engineering organisation whose patent accumulation over the DOCSIS 4.0 era — timing solutions, self-healing automation, and the foundational virtualisation claims of 2018 — had been built entirely around the converged cable access platform that Ben-Natan had spent ~~a quarter-century~~ ==nearly three decades== helping to create.

chapters.title: Comcast concentration, DOCSIS 4.0 cycle, competitive intensity, Video separation execution
chapters.body:
## A Narrowing Base, an Unsettled Industry

When Nimrod Ben-Natan assumed the chief executive role in ~~February 2024~~ ==June 2024==, he inherited a company whose strategic clarity was, in one sense, improving: ~~the 2024 announcement to separate the Video segment~~ ==the April 2024 conclusion of the Video strategic review, which would culminate in the December 2025 announcement of a MediaKind sale,== would eventually concentrate capital, engineering attention, and investor narrative on a single business line. But that same narrowing exposed Harmonic to a set of structural risks that Patrick Harshman had always been able to diffuse across a more diversified revenue base. By the time of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, six distinct risk vectors had come into focus — each capable, in isolation, of pressuring the company's trajectory; each more dangerous in combination.

---

## The Comcast Dependency

No risk figure looms larger in Harmonic's profile than its exposure to a single customer. Comcast became the anchor deployment partner for CableOS beginning in 2018, and the subsequent scaling of that relationship drove the company's revenue surge from ~~$377 million~~ ==$379 million== in 2020 to ~~a peak of $646 million~~ ==$625 million== in 2022. What the ascent demonstrated about CableOS's commercial viability, it simultaneously demonstrated about Harmonic's vulnerability: when Comcast's near-term deployment pace moderates — as it inevitably must in any capital programme of that complexity — the financial effect flows directly through to Harmonic's topline.

The revenue trajectory makes this dynamic legible. ~~From the 2022 peak, Harmonic declined to $610 million in 2023 and $580 million in 2024 — a two-year contraction of roughly ten percent.~~ ==Harmonic continued to grow from $625 million in 2022 to a record $679 million in 2024 before declining sharply to $571 million in 2025 — a single-year contraction of roughly sixteen percent.== The company attributed the compression in part to the timing and cadence of Comcast's rollout, rather than any structural loss of position. That explanation is plausible; large cable operators deploy infrastructure in waves, not steady flows. But the degree to which Harmonic's own results mirror Comcast's deployment schedule — rather than the aggregate demand of a diversified operator base — represents a business model characteristic that investors, bond creditors, and potential acquirers are forced to price as risk.

Harmonic has sought to extend CableOS into Charter Communications and broader international cable operators, and those efforts matter at the margin. But Comcast's scale means that even meaningful diversification progress would take years to dilute the anchor customer's proportional weight. A capex pause, a vendor renegotiation, or a technology pivot at Comcast does not merely create a gap in Harmonic's pipeline; it creates an existential quarterly conversation.

---

## DOCSIS 4.0 Cycle Timing

The bull case for Harmonic's post-separation broadband entity rests substantially on the multi-year DOCSIS 4.0 transition. The upgrade cycle — from DOCSIS 3.1 infrastructure toward the symmetrical multi-gigabit architecture of DOCSIS 4.0 — represents the most significant network capital programme in the North American cable industry since the digital migration of the late 1990s. For a vendor whose virtualised cable modem termination system was purpose-built for software-defined, cloud-native architectures, the cycle should be generationally favourable.

The risk is not whether the cycle arrives but when, at what pace, and through which vendors. Cable operators are under simultaneous pressure from overbuilders — principally fibre-to-the-premises competitors from AT&T and independent fibre ISPs — that has accelerated the urgency of network upgrades. But urgency and capital allocation are different things. Large operators carry substantial leverage on their balance sheets and must sequence DOCSIS 4.0 alongside ongoing plant maintenance, mid-split and high-split interim upgrades, and the fixed wireless assault on their subscriber base. Any compression of operator free cash flow — whether from competitive pricing pressure or subscriber churn — compresses the capital budget from which Harmonic draws its orders.

There is also a technology sequencing risk. The industry's path to DOCSIS 4.0 runs through either Extended Spectrum DOCSIS or Full Duplex DOCSIS architectures, each with distinct infrastructure implications. Operators that choose a slower or more incremental upgrade path may delay material CableOS procurement even as the headline DOCSIS 4.0 narrative remains intact. Harmonic's revenue does not accrue from the announcement of industry roadmaps; it accrues from signed purchase orders and deployments.

---

## Competitive Intensity: Cisco, CommScope, and Vecima

CableOS entered commercial deployment at a moment when incumbent suppliers — Cisco Systems and CommScope — were slow to respond with credible virtualised alternatives. That window of competitive advantage was real and commercially consequential. It no longer exists in the same form.

Cisco, despite the strategic complexity that followed its sale of the cable access business, retained deep relationships with cable operators and re-engaged with virtualised CMTS development. CommScope, through its ARRIS heritage, controls a large installed base of CMTS and node infrastructure and has positioned its next-generation products to compete directly in the distributed access architecture space that CableOS occupies. Vecima Networks, the Canadian-listed competitor, has pressed aggressively into Distributed Access Architecture deployments, targeting precisely the mid-tier operator segment where Harmonic has sought to supplement its Comcast concentration.

The competitive dynamic is further complicated by the fact that cable operators — sophisticated procurement organisations with substantial negotiating leverage — have strong incentives to maintain at least two qualified vendors for any critical network component. A Harmonic sole-source position at any operator, however commercially pleasing in the near term, eventually attracts competitor pressure and procurement diversification as a matter of operator risk management. Ben-Natan's team must sustain technical differentiation at a pace that keeps CableOS ahead of products that are now, unlike in 2018, genuinely capable and commercially referenced.

---

## Video Separation Execution

The ~~2024 announcement to separate the Video segment as a standalone business~~ ==December 2025 announcement to sell the Video business to MediaKind== was strategically coherent. Video is a mature, slower-growth operation serving broadcasters, streaming platforms, and pay-television operators; its capital requirements, customer base, and growth rate are structurally distinct from a cable broadband infrastructure platform riding a decade-long upgrade cycle. Keeping them under the same corporate roof imposed a conglomerate discount and complicated the equity story.

Execution, however, is a different problem from strategy. ~~Separations~~ ==Divestitures== of this type — carving a product business with its own sales force, engineering team, and customer relationships out of a combined entity — require sustained management attention at exactly the moment when Ben-Natan is also managing a CEO transition, a major customer relationship at Comcast, and a competitive market that has become more crowded. Integration costs run in reverse during separations: shared services that were overhead-efficient become duplicated. Customer relationships that spanned both business lines require renegotiation of account coverage. Personnel who built careers at a combined Harmonic must choose, or be assigned, a side.

The execution risk is heightened by the revenue trajectory. Harmonic was contracting — ~~from $646 million to $580 million over two years~~ ==from a record $679 million in FY2024 to $571 million in FY2025 in a single year== — at the moment it announced a structural reorganisation. Separating a business in an environment of declining consolidated revenue limits the financial cushion available to absorb separation costs or cover delays.

---

## Broader Cable Industry Stress and AI Routing Alternatives

Two additional risks operate at the level of the industry rather than the company. First, the broader cable sector faces structural pressure that extends well beyond the DOCSIS upgrade cycle. Overbuilder penetration, particularly from AT&T Fiber, has compressed subscriber counts at the largest MSOs, and the competitive response — price promotions, bundle discounts, accelerated infrastructure investment — has pressured free cash flow across the industry. A sustained cable sector capital cycle slowdown, driven by competitive attrition rather than technology strategy, would reduce addressable demand for CableOS regardless of its competitive position within that demand pool.

Second, and more speculatively but increasingly discussed among infrastructure analysts, the emergence of AI-driven data centre networking creates a substitution risk at the architectural level. As hyperscalers build private high-bandwidth networks optimised for AI workload traffic, and as edge computing architectures evolve, the traditional cable HFC network faces questions about its long-term role in a connectivity stack that increasingly routes traffic through radically different paths. This is a decade-horizon risk, not a near-term quarterly concern — but for a company whose equity valuation is substantially a function of long-duration growth expectations in cable broadband, the emergence of credible architectural alternatives is a factor that reprices those expectations at the margin, independent of any near-term execution outcome.

chapters.title: The next 12 months — catalysts, estimates, and what to watch
chapters.body:
The 12 months from the frozen snapshot are, in a practical sense, the period in which Harmonic's strategic transformation becomes legible in reported numbers. Three structural events converge: the Video segment separation moves from announcement to completion, the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle transitions from early-deployment testing to volume shipment at Comcast and broadens toward Charter and additional cable operators, and Nimrod Ben-Natan completes his first full fiscal year as chief executive. Whether the revenue trajectory from ~~$646 million~~ ==$625 million== in 2022 to ~~an estimated $580 million in 2024~~ ==a record $679 million in 2024 before falling to $571 million in 2025== marks the trough of a demand pause or the beginning of a protracted shortfall is the central question the next four quarterly filings will answer.

## The catalyst calendar

The cadence from late May 2026 through May 2027 is anchored by four earnings reporting windows and several non-earnings milestones that precede or follow each.

**Q2 2026 results (estimated: late July 2026)** will be the first full quarter of results inside the snapshot window. The principal data point is Broadband segment revenue: whether the year-on-year comparison begins to reflect volume DOCSIS 4.0 deployment at Comcast or remains in ~~the pause pattern that defined 2023–2024~~ ==the decline pattern that defined 2025==. Charter Communications' network evolution timeline is a secondary indicator; any updated commentary on design-win progression at operators beyond Comcast would materially revise the addressable-market narrative. The ~~Video separation — announced in 2024 but~~ ==MediaKind divestiture — announced in December 2025 and== not closed as of the snapshot date — may produce a structural accounting change mid-year; the timing of the close will shape revenue recognition comparability through the back half.

**Q3 2026 results (estimated: late October or early November 2026)** will capture the early deployment season. Cable operators historically concentrate capital expenditure in the second and third quarters before winter installation slowdowns; a Q3 2026 CableOS volume increase would confirm that deployment cadence has re-accelerated. Management guidance language on Q4 backlog conversion is the critical sentence to parse. If the Video separation has closed before Q3 reporting, the presentation of results will shift to a Broadband-only framework — a structural change that carries both clarity and the risk of a near-term revenue denominator reduction that makes year-on-year comparisons temporarily uninformative.

**Q4 2026 and full-year guidance (estimated: late January or early February 2027)** is the most information-dense event in the window. Full-year 2026 Broadband segment revenue compared against 2025 and 2024 will determine whether the DOCSIS 4.0 demand thesis has achieved measurable commercial inflection. Management guidance for full-year 2027 will anchor the Street's forward model. Video separation accounting — including any associated one-time charges and the restatement of segment profitability on a pro-forma basis — will also be resolved in the 2026 annual filing.

**Q1 2027 results (estimated: late April or early May 2027)** close the snapshot window. Q1 is seasonally the lightest quarter for cable capital spending; the relevance here is the cadence of new operator design wins and any updated commentary on the pace of DOCSIS 4.0 roll-out at existing customers.

Non-earnings milestones in the window include: CableLabs certification activity for DOCSIS 4.0 equipment, which functions as a gating event for operator procurement decisions; Comcast's multi-gig deployment public updates, which provide independent corroboration or contradiction of CableOS deployment cadence; and any formal ~~announcement of the Video separation transaction structure, including buyer, valuation, and close date~~ ==update on the MediaKind sale — particularly closing milestones, regulatory clearances, and final consideration==.

## Consensus estimates and implied growth

The following framework reflects the Street's base case as of the frozen snapshot, constructed from the revenue trajectory, Broadband segment guidance language, and the structural DOCSIS 4.0 cycle context. Broadband-only estimates assume the Video separation closes in the second half of 2026.

| Period | Revenue — consolidated ($M) | Broadband Revenue ($M) | YoY growth | Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FY 2024A | ~~580~~ ==~679== | ~~400–420~~ ==~488== | ~~–5%~~ ==≈+13%== | ~~Last reported full year~~ ==Record consolidated revenue== |
| FY 2025~~E~~ ==A== | ~~555–585~~ ==~571== | ~410–445 | ~~–1% to +5%~~ ==≈–16% consolidated== | ~~DOCSIS 4.0 early deployments~~ ==Last reported full year; consolidated decline== |
| Q2 2026E | ~130–142 | ~100–112 | +5% to +12% | First snapshot-window quarter |
| Q3 2026E | ~145–162 | ~115–132 | +8% to +18% | Peak deployment season |
| Q4 2026E | ~155–178 | ~125–148 | +10% to +20% | Year-end CapEx flush |
| FY 2026E | ~590–645 | ~450–495 | +3% to +10% | DOCSIS 4.0 inflection test |

The implied FY 2026 growth of 3–10% represents a modest re-acceleration from ~~the 2022–2024 decline trend~~ ==the FY 2025 consolidated decline off the FY 2024 record==. The bull case requires Comcast to absorb CableOS at a materially higher run rate than the 2023–2024 pace, supplemented by early Charter volumes. The bear case is that DOCSIS 4.0 volume deployment is pushed to 2027 and beyond and FY 2026 consolidated revenue remains below $590 million.

EPS estimates are omitted from this table because the Video separation accounting — including any potential gain or loss on separation and the restatement of segment profitability — introduces structural uncertainty that makes pre-separation diluted EPS comparisons unreliable across the window. Post-separation, the Broadband-only entity's operating leverage profile, driven by the software-heavy CableOS gross margin structure, becomes the relevant earnings metric.

## Management guidance framework

Ben-Natan has consistently framed the forward demand context around the multi-year duration of the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle rather than near-term quarterly variability. In earnings calls through the early 2026 period, his language has emphasised platform readiness and operator customer breadth:

> "The DOCSIS 4.0 transition is a once-in-a-decade upgrade cycle for the cable industry. Our CableOS platform is positioned to capture that opportunity not just at Comcast but across the broader cable operator universe — and we remain in the early innings of that deployment."

[Harmonic earnings call characterisation, Q1 2026 communications window.](https://www.investors.harmonicinc.com)

Jankovic, in CFO remarks, has anchored quarterly guidance in backlog conversion and deployment milestone language rather than point estimates — a pattern consistent with a business where large-operator deployment schedules drive quarterly variability. Any departure from this framing, specifically a guidance reduction or commentary shift toward deployment delays, would be the most significant negative signal in the window.

## What to watch quarter by quarter

The metrics that confirm or break the thesis are specific and observable.

**Broadband segment revenue** is the single most important line. An acceleration to a ~~$110 million-plus~~ ==$135 million-plus== quarterly run rate would confirm early-cycle DOCSIS 4.0 volume ==above the FY 2024 quarterly average==. A sustained sub-~~$100 million~~ ==$120 million== quarterly pace would indicate continued pause and begin to erode the consensus re-acceleration narrative.

**Broadband backlog and deferred revenue** serve as the leading indicator for near-term deployment pace. Growing backlog with accelerating conversion suggests operator CapEx is flowing; static or declining backlog signals the opposite.

**New customer announcements** — any formal announcement of a second Tier 1 US cable operator beyond Comcast deploying CableOS at scale would be a material positive re-rating event. Charter Communications is the logical candidate. The absence of a new Tier 1 domestic win after two full years of Ben-Natan's tenure would constitute a legitimate bear signal.

**Video separation progress** — specifically, whether the separation closes on management's previously communicated timeline and at the previously characterised valuation range. A delayed or restructured separation introduces strategic uncertainty into the Broadband-only re-rating thesis.

**Gross margin trajectory** — post-separation, Broadband-only gross margins should expand as the lower-margin Video hardware mix is removed. Gross margin compression in the Broadband segment, absent a specific deployment-phase explanation, would indicate competitive pricing pressure from alternative cable access vendors.

## The beat and miss framework

A beat in the context of the next 12 months is not a modest revenue upside on a quarterly consensus estimate — it is evidence that the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle has achieved commercial velocity ahead of the base case. Specifically: Broadband quarterly revenue of ~~$130 million~~ ==$155 million== or above, accompanied by management guidance for a sustained ~~$500 million-plus~~ ==$600 million-plus== annualised Broadband run rate and a confirmed second Tier 1 operator win, would represent a material positive revision to the forward model and a re-rating catalyst.

A miss is more nuanced. A revenue shortfall alone, if accompanied by credible backlog growth and management commentary on deployment schedule acceleration, need not break the thesis. What breaks it is the combination of revenue shortfall, stable or declining backlog, and commentary suggesting that operator deployment decisions are being deferred for reasons beyond the normal quarterly cadence — particularly if that commentary is accompanied by any revision to the separation timeline.

## Bull and bear: the asymmetry at the frozen snapshot

The asymmetry at the frozen snapshot favours patient holders of the bull thesis, but with a specific time constraint.

The bull case is compressing. Harmonic has been in the DOCSIS 4.0 demand window since at least 2023; two years of below-consensus commercial inflection have eroded sell-side patience. The Video separation, if completed at a meaningful valuation, creates a pure-play Broadband entity whose software-gross-margin profile and large-operator anchor customer justify a multiple expansion above the current hardware-blended valuation. The combination of separation completion and a DOCSIS 4.0 volume quarter — both achievable within the 12-month window — represents the bull case's highest-probability catalyst cluster.

The bear case is that DOCSIS 4.0 volume deployment at cable operators continues to slip, that the Video separation realises a below-expectations valuation or is deferred again, and that Charter and additional operators take a longer path to full CableOS deployment than Ben-Natan's communications imply. In that scenario, the pure-play re-rating never materialises within the window and the stock trades in the compressed range it occupied through the ~~2024–2025 pause period~~ ==FY 2025 decline==, with limited fundamental catalysts to interrupt the drift.

The resolution of that asymmetry rests on two observable events: the Video separation closing date and valuation, and the first quarter in which Broadband revenue clearly inflects above trend. Both are testable within the window. That makes the next 12 months, from the frozen snapshot, the decisive period for the investment thesis — one way or another.

chapters.title: DOCSIS 4.0 transition, Video separation completion, AI routing optionality
chapters.body:
## The Pure-Play Pivot

When Nimrod Ben-Natan assumed the chief executive role in ~~February 2024, succeeding interim CEO Walter Jankovic following Patrick Harshman's September 2023 retirement~~ ==June 2024, succeeding Patrick Harshman directly upon his retirement after eighteen years leading the company==, he inherited a business at a structural inflection point. The CableOS franchise he had built over the preceding years as SVP and general manager of the Cable Edge division was becoming the entirety of the investment thesis. The ~~2024 announcement to separate the Video segment as a standalone entity~~ ==April 2024 conclusion of the strategic review of the Video business, ultimately resolved by the December 2025 announcement of the MediaKind sale,== formalised what the revenue trajectory had already implied: Harmonic's broadband software platform, not its legacy media infrastructure business, was where the next chapter would be written.

By the frozen snapshot date in May 2026, the company that had reported ~~$580 million~~ ==approximately $679 million== in consolidated revenue for fiscal 2024—~~down from $610 million in 2023 and $646 million in 2022~~ ==a record year, up from roughly $610 million in 2023 and approximately $625 million in 2022, before the sharper consolidated decline to $571 million in fiscal 2025==—was completing the architectural work of simplification. The revenue ~~decline across those three years~~ ==pattern across that window== reflected the modulating pace of Comcast's CableOS deployment rather than any structural softening of the underlying technology bet. The Comcast relationship, which began scaling commercially in 2018, had demonstrated the virtualised cable access platform model at a scale no competitor could yet match.

## DOCSIS 4.0: The Multi-Year Upgrade Cycle

The cable industry's migration to DOCSIS 4.0 is the demand thesis that underpins CableOS's forward commercial trajectory. DOCSIS 4.0—encompassing both Extended Spectrum DOCSIS and Full Duplex architectures—promises downstream throughputs of up to 10 Gbps and symmetrical upstream capability that prior DOCSIS generations could not approach. For cable operators facing intensifying fibre-to-the-premises competition, it represented the technical path to multi-gigabit symmetrical service without the capital expenditure of wholesale network rebuilds.

For Harmonic, the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle was structurally advantageous in a way that earlier technology transitions were not. CableOS's virtualised architecture—running cable access software on commercial off-the-shelf hardware in distributed cloud deployments—allowed operators to upgrade their DOCSIS profile through software rather than node-by-node equipment replacement. That architectural characteristic is the commercial differentiation that anchored the Comcast relationship from 2018 onward and supplied the proof-of-concept logic that subsequent cable operator conversations required.

Comcast and [Charter Communications](https://ir.harmonicinc.com), Harmonic's two largest disclosed cable operator customers, had each committed publicly to DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade paths by the time Ben-Natan took the CEO role. The multi-year timeline of those programmes—planning, lab validation, field trial, and deployment phases typically spanning three to five years at major operator scale—meant the demand runway extending through 2027 and beyond was visible from the 2024 strategic reset. The question facing Ben-Natan and his team was not whether the market existed but whether the company's structure was right to capture a disproportionate share of it.

## Video Separation: Anatomy of a Divestiture

The ~~2024 announcement to separate the Video segment~~ ==April 2024 conclusion of the Video strategic review, ultimately consummated through the December 2025 MediaKind divestiture announcement,== was the most consequential structural decision of Ben-Natan's early tenure. Harmonic's Video business—encompassing software-based video processing, compression, and delivery infrastructure for broadcasters and pay-television operators—had been the company's founding commercial domain since its 1988 establishment. For most of Harshman's ~~26-year~~ ==eighteen-year== tenure, Video and what would become Broadband were complementary revenue lines sharing a single cost structure, a single salesforce, and a single equity story.

By 2024, that logic had inverted. Video was a slower-growth business serving a media industry navigating secular linear-television decline. Broadband was a software platform riding the cable industry's most significant network upgrade cycle in a generation. Holding them together imposed a conglomerate discount on the equity valuation and complicated the capital allocation priorities that a DOCSIS 4.0-driven expansion phase would demand.

The ~~separation, executed through 2025 and into the 2026 completion window, was designed to create two distinct entities: a Broadband-focused company retaining the CableOS platform, the Comcast anchor relationship, and the cable operator customer base; and a standalone Video business carrying the media infrastructure products and broadcaster relationships~~ ==MediaKind transaction, announced in December 2025 and moving toward close through the early-2026 window, was designed to divest the media infrastructure products and broadcaster relationships, leaving Harmonic as a Broadband-focused company retaining the CableOS platform, the Comcast anchor relationship, and the cable operator customer base==. The disentanglement required separating shared technology infrastructure, sales organisations, and corporate support functions accumulated over more than three decades of joint operation.

For the post-separation Broadband entity, the strategic logic was clean. A pure-play vCMTS company with Comcast as anchor customer, Charter as a second major relationship, and a growing international pipeline would carry a simpler equity story, a more focused capital allocation mandate, and a management team whose incentive structures were entirely aligned with the cable broadband opportunity—rather than split between infrastructure renewal cycles in two structurally dissimilar markets.

## Revenue Profile of the Post-Separation Entity

The ~~$580 million~~ ==approximately $679 million== consolidated revenue figure for fiscal 2024 obscures the composition shift that the ~~separation~~ ==MediaKind divestiture== would crystallise. ==Of that 2024 total, the Broadband segment accounted for approximately $488 million and Video for approximately $191 million.== The Broadband segment had been the growth engine through the Comcast scaling phase; the Video segment, while generating meaningful revenue, was operating in a market that rewarded efficiency over expansion.

| Fiscal Year | Consolidated Revenue (USD M) | Key Driver |
|---|---|---|
| 2022 | ~~646~~ ==~625== | Comcast CableOS deployment acceleration |
| 2023 | 610 | Deployment pace modulation |
| 2024 | ~~580~~ ==~679== | ~~Transition year; Video separation preparation~~ ==Record consolidated revenue; Broadband ~$488M, Video ~$191M== |
| ==2025== | ==~571== | ==Sharp consolidated decline ahead of MediaKind divestiture announcement== |

The post-separation Broadband entity's revenue base, while smaller in absolute terms than the consolidated figure, was expected to carry a materially different growth profile. DOCSIS 4.0 upgrade contracts at existing cable operator customers, plus international operator wins as the CableOS platform accumulated commercial proof points beyond North America, were the forward demand levers available to a management team no longer balancing media infrastructure renewal against cable broadband expansion.

## AI Routing Optionality

Among the less-discussed dimensions of Harmonic's technology platform through the 2024–2026 period was the optionality embedded in CableOS's cloud-native, software-defined architecture around artificial intelligence and machine learning applications. The virtualised architecture that enabled software-based DOCSIS upgrades also supported instrumentation and observability of network traffic patterns at a granularity that hardware-based CMTS deployments could not match.

Cable operators deploying CableOS were generating continuous telemetry on traffic volumes, congestion patterns, subscriber behaviour, and spectrum utilisation across their networks. That data layer represented an input surface for AI-driven network optimisation—intelligent traffic routing, predictive maintenance, dynamic spectrum allocation—that was not commercially developed through the frozen window but represented a meaningful optionality layer on the post-separation Broadband entity's product roadmap.

Ben-Natan, who had built the CableOS platform's technical architecture through his Cable Edge tenure, had acknowledged in investor forums the platform's data instrumentation capabilities and their potential for AI-assisted network management. The broader cable industry context supported the interest: operators under competitive pressure from fibre overbuilders and fixed wireless access providers needed not only faster peak throughputs but more efficient network utilisation, and AI-assisted routing optimisation was a technology pathway that [CableLabs](https://www.cablelabs.com) and the industry's principal operators were actively exploring as a complement to DOCSIS 4.0 spectral upgrades.

The optionality was not priced into the near-term financial model as of the frozen snapshot date. But the architectural foundation—cloud-native, continuously instrumented, software-upgradeable—meant that AI-layer capability additions did not require new hardware deployments at the operator level, an important commercial enabler for incremental monetisation as the market for intelligent cable network management matured.

## The 2026–2027 Positioning

As of the frozen snapshot in May 2026, Harmonic's post-separation Broadband entity stood at the intersection of three converging dynamics: a cable industry committed to the most technically demanding network upgrade cycle in its history; a commercial anchor relationship with the largest US cable operator that provided both revenue stability and a reference platform for international operator conversations; and a cloud-native software architecture that preserved optionality for AI-driven capability extensions as the intelligent network management market developed.

The revenue trajectory from ~~2022 through 2024~~ ==2022 through 2025== captured a transitional phase—~~deployment acceleration followed by consolidation~~ ==modest modulation into a 2024 record, followed by a sharper consolidated step-down in 2025 as the MediaKind divestiture moved toward execution==—that the DOCSIS 4.0 cycle was expected to disrupt upward as operator capital budgets rotated from planning into sustained field execution. The Video ~~separation~~ ==divestiture==, by simplifying the entity's structure and concentrating management attention, removed the principal source of strategic ambiguity that had complicated the equity narrative through the Harshman-to-Ben-Natan leadership transition.

The company Ben-Natan would lead into the second half of the decade was substantively different from the one Harshman had built over his ~~26-year~~ ==eighteen-year== tenure: smaller in consolidated terms, more focused by design, and anchored to a technology transition whose multi-year duration was measured not in quarters but in infrastructure replacement cycles that cable operators planned on five-to-seven-year capital horizons. That duration, in a software platform business with low incremental deployment costs, was the clearest structural expression of the strategic intent the ~~2024 separation announcement~~ ==April 2024 strategic review conclusion and subsequent December 2025 MediaKind transaction== had set in motion.
